It would help to define more concrete indicators for what counts as an APA error (in-text citation formatting, reference list formatting, p-value formatting, spacing) versus a language/structure issue. The band descriptions could also specify whether frequency or severity should dominate when errors are mixed (e.g., many minor typos plus a few major APA/statistical-format violations). Finally, the rubric would benefit from examples for “single focus and topical sentences” versus “unstructured paragraphs” at the paragraph level.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides a broad overview of SAD, exposure-based CBT, and introduces VRET and the motivation for therapist-guided vs self-guided formats. It includes several relevant theoretical ideas (exposure mechanisms, Bandura self-efficacy, Vygotsky interaction/zone of proximal development) and attempts to justify the need for more accessible therapy. However, the research gap and research question are not clearly and crisply formulated until the very end, and the logic linking the theories to specific, testable hypotheses is often asserted rather than systematically derived. The prior research synthesis is present but uneven: key studies are summarized without consistently extracting the exact implications for the present design (e.g., what is controlled, what mechanism is isolated), and several claims are unclear or contain incorrect/inconsistent referencing details.
intro_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but has frequent grammatical/word-choice issues (e.g., “people their,” “TVRET condition,” “their comfort zone,” “rate that therapists ask for their help”). APA/academic style is inconsistent: some citations are missing years/appropriate formatting (e.g., “National Institute of Mental Health. z.d.”), and author/year usage varies (“Patel et al. 2022” vs “Patel, 2022”). Paragraphing is inconsistent, with very long paragraphs and some unclear transitions between societal relevance, theory, prior research, and the stated purpose/hypotheses. There are multiple spelling/capitalization inconsistencies (e.g., “TVRET,” “VRET-sessions,” “Dass-21,” “Vygotsky, 1978”) and occasional imprecise wording that would make later argumentation harder to follow.
intro_rubric_feedback: The rubric criteria would benefit from clearer, more concrete thresholds for what counts as a “clear and appropriate” research question and hypothesis vs merely an asserted purpose. Also, the distinction between “somewhat coherent” and “mostly coherent” argumentation is currently too interpretive—adding examples of specific missing argumentation steps (e.g., missing linkage from theory → hypothesis → operationalization) would improve reliability. Finally, the rubric could specify how to judge “references relevant and up to date” when the student uses many sources but several contain questionable or mismatched details; a rule for weighting reference quality vs quantity would make the Introduction scoring more consistent.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section identifies the main study components (diagnosed SAD participants, VR exposure delivered via a headset, LSAS-SR as the outcome, and a 10-week treatment period with therapist contact in one condition and not in the other). However, key design details needed to replicate the study are missing or unclear: the sample size in each condition, the exact random allocation procedure, and the treatment dose/structure for SVRET vs TVRET are inconsistently specified. The materials description includes some plausible scenario details and references, but key implementation details are absent (e.g., how the “listeners” were instructed, whether exposure intensity/difficulty was standardized, and what “therapist on call” means operationally). The outcome measurement description is also partly inaccurate/unclear (e.g., multiple regression is mentioned without any corresponding results/analysis plan, and scoring details are inconsistent with the LSAS-SR structure).
methods_style_notes: The section is readable but frequently imprecise (e.g., “measured with VR headset” and “statistics done through multiple regression” without stating an analysis plan). There are multiple grammar issues and awkward phrasing (“VR-listeners could be instructed…”, “program used, used before”), plus an occasional spelling/notation problem (SVRET/TVRET inconsistency; mismatched parentheses around citations). APA-wise, citations are not consistently formatted (spacing and placement), and there are at least a few unclear constructs/terms that could be tightened into standard academic wording. Paragraphing is present but often the sentences mix description of procedure, materials, and scoring rules, reducing clarity.
methods_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s Method criteria focus on coherence with the stated RQ/hypotheses and on whether participants/materials/procedure are described comprehensibly and completely. However, distinguishing “complete and correct” from “mostly complete and mostly correct” is difficult without explicitly listing which concrete sub-items must appear (e.g., exact N per condition, randomization method, allocation concealment, assessment time points). Also, the rubric combines “participants/materials/procedures completeness” with “study design coherence” in a way that can overlap with Results/Discussion expectations. Adding a short checklist of mandatory replication-critical elements (N per arm, inclusion/exclusion detail, recruitment/consent, randomization, intervention fidelity/dose, and analytic plan at least at the level of tests) would make the scoring bands more separable and more consistent between graders.
results_content_summary: The section reports a 2 (time) × 3 (condition) mixed ANOVA on LSAS with assumption checks (normality via Q-Q plot; homogeneity via Levene’s test) and provides main effects and the time × condition interaction, plus Holm-corrected post-hoc comparisons. However, the degrees of freedom and the ANOVA structure are inconsistent with a 3-level between-subjects factor (reporting F(1, 99) for both main effects and interaction, which does not match a 2×3 design). Several post-hoc results also appear contradictory or unclear (e.g., similar non-significant p-values for different comparisons, “waitlist did not improve” while an earlier main effect of time is significant, and formatting issues like p = <.001). Overall, while the intended analysis is relevant, the reporting is incomplete/incorrect enough to prevent a solid, rubric-level confirmation of statistical reasoning and alignment with the stated methods.
results_style_notes: Clarity is limited by frequent formatting problems (missing leading zeros, inconsistent spacing, and use of p = <.001 / p  < .001). APA/statistical notation is inconsistent (e.g., F(1, 99) despite a 3-condition factor) and tables/figures are referenced without the actual descriptive results being shown in this excerpt. Paragraphing is mostly present, but sentences become long and run together around key inferential statements, making it harder to follow. There are also several capitalization/terminology inconsistencies (SVRET/TVRET vs “Self-led/Therapist-led”) and unclear wording (“both assumptions met…” without test statistics).
results_rubric_feedback: The Results criterion distinguishes “correct/incomplete” from “mostly correct/complete,” but it lacks concrete anchors for when an analysis is deemed wrong vs merely underreported; adding explicit examples (e.g., mismatched df for the stated design) would improve reliability. The phrase “in terms of stated design and procedure” is helpful but could specify which elements (factor count, dfs, tests, correction method) are mandatory to avoid over/under-penalizing. The band descriptors for statistical reasoning (e.g., “demonstrating in depth knowledge”) are also vague; including a short checklist of reportable items (e.g., effect sizes, df consistency, post-hoc structure) would make grading thresholds more transparent.
discussion_content_summary: The discussion attempts to answer the research question by comparing SVRET/TVRET to waitlist and interprets the main finding that SVRET outperformed TVRET. It connects results to prior studies and offers theoretical explanations using Bandura’s self-efficacy and Vygotsky’s interaction/zone of proximal development, but these links are often vague and sometimes misframed (e.g., “in line with interaction theory” yet concluding evidence supports only self-efficacy). The section includes multiple limitations and future research ideas, yet several are generic or not tightly grounded in the reported design (e.g., follow-up expectations, manipulations/assumptions not actually tested). Overall, the reasoning and use of literature are inconsistent, and the discussion does not clearly and convincingly integrate findings, theory, and study-specific methodological constraints.
discussion_style_notes: Language is understandable but repeatedly contains inaccuracies and imprecisions (e.g., variable naming confusion such as SVRET/TVRET/TVRET into in vivo; “SVRET works well” phrasing; “SVRET into in vivo” constructions; multiple year/author mismatches). Paragraphing is uneven with long blocks and abrupt transitions; several sentences lack clear grammar/structure, and there are multiple punctuation/spacing issues. APA compliance appears weak in this section (inconsistent citation formatting, missing/incorrect authors’ years in a few places, and an informal final conclusion). There is also some redundancy (re-stating outcomes and hypotheses) and several unclear or overly definite claims without corresponding support from the presented results.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The rubric could better distinguish between (a) correct identification of expected vs unexpected findings and (b) depth/grounding of interpretation in the study’s actual design and data. The Discussion criteria currently bundles “critical reflection,” “responsible references,” and “outstanding insight” into broad bands; adding subcriteria or examples would help graders separate an adequate limitation list from a genuinely study-specific critique. The language/style threshold for Discussion (“vague or ambiguous statements in crucial parts”) is hard to operationalize—adding clearer examples of what counts as “crucial parts” and what is considered a “vague statement” would improve reliability. Finally, the rubric might specify how to handle theory links that are present but logically misaligned (e.g., claiming alignment with a theory despite contradictory phrasing), because this is a common failure mode at this level.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric would benefit from clearer, more concrete thresholds for what counts as “vague or ambiguous statements” and how to judge whether they are “crucial parts.” The current error-count cutoffs (e.g., grammar/spelling, APA/layout) are useful but could be harmonized with guidance on whether severe citation/statistical-format issues should outweigh higher minor error counts. It may also help to define “clearly structured (single focus and topical sentences)” in operational terms (e.g., how many sentences/ideas per paragraph). Finally, consider adding an explicit descriptor for inconsistency in construct naming/labeling (important for understanding) rather than leaving it implicit under “impedes proper understanding.”

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides a general overview of SAD, exposure therapy, and VRET, and it includes several citations to justify why the topic matters. However, the scientific storyline leading to a clear, testable research question and hypothesis is incomplete: the final hypothesis is stated, but the theoretical reasoning (Bandura/interaction theory) is not clearly linked to specific, measurable constructs in your intended design. Prior research is summarized, but the synthesis is often inconsistent and sometimes introduces confounds (e.g., CBT, group vs individual therapy, in vivo transition) without fully translating those points into a precise gap and study purpose. Overall, the introduction is understandable, but the argumentation is not consistently coherent enough to meet the rubric’s “line of reasoning culminating in the RQ and hypothesis” standard.
intro_style_notes: The writing is generally readable, but there are frequent grammar/wording issues (e.g., “people their…”, inconsistent capitalization such as TVRET/TVRET/VRET/SVRET, and several awkward or incorrect phrases). APA compliance is weak: several citations are incorrectly formatted or missing year formatting, and there are numerous inconsistent citation styles (e.g., “et al, 2004” vs “et al. 2017”, mixed punctuation, and inconsistent organization of in-text citations). Paragraph structure is uneven: long sections combine multiple concepts and claims without clear topical sentence focus, and there is redundancy in explaining exposure principles and access/waitlists multiple times.
intro_rubric_feedback: Consider tightening the rubric distinctions between (a) a “clear but somewhat vague” RQ and (b) a “somewhat coherent storyline” that is present but not convincing—right now those bands overlap. Adding a sub-criterion about whether the hypothesis is explicitly derived from the stated theory (not just mentioned) would make grading more consistent. Also, the rubric could clarify what counts as “more than half references irrelevant or outdated”: for example, whether non-peer-reviewed sources or missing/unclear APA-formatted citations should be treated separately from relevance/recency. Finally, adding concrete examples of “testable and logically derived hypotheses” vs “somewhat testable” would help raters apply thresholds more uniformly.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section describes the target population, key inclusion/exclusion criteria, a basic description of the VR headset and scenario content, the main dependent measure (LSAS), and a clear outline of the treatment timeline (10 weeks, weekly sessions, plus therapist “on call” vs planned therapist sessions). However, several critical replication details are missing or unclear, especially regarding allocation procedure (randomization method), what “comorbidities” means, what constitutes sufficient Dutch, and how therapist guidance is operationalized in SVRET vs TVRET. The materials section also contains confusing wording (e.g., “SVRET/TVRET” labels, listener reactions not clearly tied to condition, and scenario-development claims), and the description of the data analysis is not consistent with the methods you would need for a design like this (e.g., “multiple regression” is stated, but the design implies pre/post comparisons across three groups). Overall, the methods are partially coherent with the stated research aim (guidance mode and symptom change), but not complete enough for a strong “adequate/good” rubric band.
methods_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but contains frequent imprecision and grammar issues (e.g., sentence fragments, inconsistent spacing around parentheses, and unclear references like “VR-listeners” and “The program used, used before”). APA formatting is inconsistent: there is no consistent use of comma placement/capitalization, citations are sometimes placed awkwardly, and key statistical/method terms (e.g., multiple regression) are mentioned without proper structure. Paragraph structure follows the expected subsections (Participants/Materials/Procedure), but within subsections there is redundancy and unclear phrasing (e.g., repeated “used before by Kan et al.” and “improvement of SAD was measured” followed immediately by item counting without transition).
methods_rubric_feedback: Your rubric could benefit from clearer thresholds for “incomplete but mostly correct” versus “nearly complete.” For example, the Methods band currently mixes two dimensions (coherence/relatedness vs completeness/details), but the rubric doesn’t specify which missing details are critical enough to drop a whole band (e.g., randomization method, operational definition of the independent variable, pre/post schedule, and analysis plan). Adding concrete examples of what counts as “one or two important details missing” would improve grader consistency. Finally, the Results rubric mentions “in-depth knowledge of statistical analyses,” but the Methods rubric does not explicitly assess whether the planned analysis matches the design—this criterion could be made more explicit (and tied to examples) to reduce ambiguity.
results_content_summary: The section reports an intended 2 (time) × 3 (condition) mixed ANOVA on LSAS scores and describes tests for normality and homogeneity (q-q plot/Levene). However, the statistical reporting is internally inconsistent: it states one between-participant factor with three conditions, yet reports F-tests with dfs consistent with a 2-level between factor (e.g., F(1, 99)), which does not match the described design. The post-hoc description is also not coherent with the earlier claims about interaction and condition effects (e.g., paired vs between-group comparisons are mixed, p-values are inconsistently formatted, and “waitlist did not improve” is asserted without a clear mean/SD table or effect direction). Overall, the results are difficult to evaluate for correctness and completeness because key outputs (means/SDs, full ANOVA table, and which post-hocs were run) are missing or ambiguous.
results_style_notes: Language is generally understandable, but there are multiple precision issues and typos/inconsistencies (e.g., SVRET vs TVRET, q-q plot vs assumed spelling, SVRET performed better than TVRET statement without supporting values). Statistical notation is inconsistently formatted (missing/uneven spaces and punctuation in p-values), and the ANOVA degrees of freedom are not presented clearly enough to verify consistency with the stated design. Paragraph structure is mostly present, but the section refers to “Table 1/Table 2” and “Figure 1” without actually including them, reducing clarity and compliance with typical results reporting conventions for this course.
results_rubric_feedback: Some rubric wording blurs what counts as “mostly correct” vs “nearly complete” for Results, especially when the reported statistics are internally inconsistent. Consider adding explicit sub-criteria about (a) whether dfs and model specification match the described design, (b) whether key descriptive outputs (means/SDs) and effect estimates are provided, and (c) whether post-hoc procedures are specified (type of comparisons, correction method, and whether comparisons address pre/post within groups or between-group at each time). Also, the rubric mentions “in-depth knowledge” but doesn’t define what level of statistical reasoning should be expected at bachelor level (e.g., checking df consistency, reporting interaction follow-ups), which can lead to inconsistent grading between graders.
discussion_content_summary: The discussion restates that both VR conditions reduced SAD symptoms and that self-led VR reportedly outperformed therapist-led VR and waitlist, and it attempts to connect these outcomes to Bandura’s self-efficacy and “interaction”/ZPD ideas. It also compares the findings to several prior studies and proposes multiple limitations (age range, lack of follow-up, and insufficient direct testing of the proposed mechanisms). However, the argumentation is internally inconsistent in places (e.g., mixing SVRET/TVRET terminology and referencing different study designs/results), and several claims about what the data do or do not show are not tightly linked to specific results from this study. Critical reflection is present but sometimes speculative, and the theoretical integration (especially the interaction theory vs the observed pattern) is not fully grounded in the study’s actual measurements/manipulation checks.
discussion_style_notes: The language is generally understandable, but frequent imprecise phrasing and grammatical errors reduce clarity (e.g., “SVRET works well… compared to TVRET” without consistent terminology; missing/incorrect punctuation and agreement). APA compliance is weak in the discussion: several citations are inconsistently formatted (missing parentheses year consistency; one citation “Linder et al, 2018” without a period) and there are stylistic inconsistencies (SVRET/TVRET/VRET references). Paragraph structure is mostly sequential (findings → prior research → theory → limitations/future research), but topical sentences are not consistently used and some paragraphs become multi-topic. There is also a notable amount of redundancy and some over-specific claims (e.g., post–follow-up expectations, effect fades) that are not anchored to the study’s reported design.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s Discussion criteria could be made more concrete by explicitly distinguishing “theory connection” quality (e.g., whether the discussion operationally ties mechanisms to measures/manipulation) from general theoretical name-dropping. Separating “unexpected findings handling” from “critical reflection depth” would also improve differentiation between “some limitations mentioned” vs “limitations that actually explain results or design weaknesses.” Finally, the rubric bands use broad qualifiers like “somewhat relevant” and “somewhat convincingly argued”; adding example cues (e.g., what counts as a responsible alternative explanation vs unsupported speculation) would help graders apply criteria consistently.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric would benefit from clearer separation between APA/formatting (which is countable) and argumentation clarity at sentence/paragraph level (which is more subjective). The thresholds such as “>10 different errors” vs “5–10” could be operationalized more explicitly (e.g., whether a single recurring issue counts once or per occurrence) to improve inter-rater reliability. Adding brief examples for each performance band (e.g., what counts as a “vague or ambiguous statement” in a crucial part) would make the criteria easier to apply consistently. Finally, the rubric could more explicitly weigh consistency of key terminology (e.g., intervention abbreviations) alongside raw error counts.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides a relevant topic (SAD, exposure/VRET, and therapist vs self-led formats) and includes several constructs and theoretical ideas (exposure principles, self-efficacy, interaction/zone of proximal development). It also discusses prior empirical studies with an attempt to identify gaps (e.g., lack of clear conclusions about pure VRET vs VRET plus in vivo, and limited testing outside public speaking). However, the research question and hypotheses are not stated in a clearly structured, testable way (e.g., outcome measures and the exact predictions/contrasts are vague), and the causal chain linking theory → specific expectations is not consistently and explicitly argued. Overall, the storyline culminates in a somewhat understandable purpose, but coherence and argument quality fall short of the rubric’s “mostly coherent and somewhat convincingly argued” requirement for this level.
intro_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but frequently contains imprecise phrasing and grammar issues (e.g., 'people their', 'TVRET' vs 'VRET', inconsistent tense, and unclear sentences). APA compliance is weak: several citations are missing proper author-year formatting (e.g., 'et al' spacing, 'National Institute of Mental Health. z.d.'), and author names/years are inconsistent across the text. Paragraph structure is uneven: the section is long with multiple topics per paragraph, and transitions are often abrupt. There is some redundancy (re-stating general accessibility/waitlist issues and self-efficacy/exposure mechanisms) without always integrating it back into the specific research gap and testable hypothesis.
intro_rubric_feedback: Consider tightening the rubric’s differentiation between “somewhat coherent and somewhat convincingly argued” versus “sound and coherent.” Many introductions can be judged similarly if they have a plausible but not fully explicit theory-to-hypothesis link; adding concrete indicators (e.g., whether the RQ/hypotheses specify groups/contrasts and predicted direction) would make that band easier to grade. Also, the rubric currently mentions “more than half of references irrelevant or outdated,” but provides no threshold for what counts as “relevant” or “outdated,” which can create inconsistent scoring; adding examples of acceptable versus unacceptable reference relevance would help. Finally, the Methods/RQ-related language could be more concrete (e.g., explicitly stating that RQ/hypotheses must be testable via the planned design), since that is a key practical skill for passing.
methods_content_summary: The methods describe the study’s broad design (participants with SAD, VR headset/program, LSAS-SR as outcome) and include some key elements like inclusion/exclusion criteria, random allocation to conditions, and timing of treatment and assessments. However, the section lacks several crucial details needed to replicate the study: group sizes per condition, the randomization process, therapist characteristics/standardization, exact intervention dose details (session lengths, frequency), and how SVRET vs TVRET differ beyond “planned vs altered.” Several statements in the methods are conceptually imprecise (e.g., “any comorbidities” without defining what is allowed, multiple regression being claimed without matching the analysis described elsewhere, and “minimal amount…maximum” scoring details presented but not clearly tied to scoring/scales and interpretation). Overall, the methods are incomplete and partly inconsistent, making it difficult to assess internal validity and to reproduce the study accurately.
methods_style_notes: The language is understandable but contains frequent grammar and phrasing issues (e.g., missing articles, inconsistent capitalization, run-on sentences, and unclear references like “the program used, used before”). APA compliance is weak: inconsistent citation formatting (“Kan et al, 2025” vs “Liebowitz, 1987”), missing italics/spacing consistency, and some unclear punctuation. Paragraph structure is present via headings, but many paragraphs contain multiple ideas without clear sub-substructure, which harms precision. There is also some redundancy and some unclear or erroneous phrasing (e.g., “multiple regression” reported in the same paragraph as LSAS scoring despite not being specified as the planned analysis).
methods_rubric_feedback: The rubric criteria could be made more distinguishable between “somewhat coherently related” and “nearly complete and mostly correct.” In the Methods band descriptors, consider explicitly listing which specific subcomponents (participants: allocation + sample characteristics; materials: intervention protocol + questionnaire scoring; procedure: assessment schedule + debriefing; analyses: statistical model) must be present for each step, instead of relying on general completeness wording. Also, add concrete examples for what counts as “important details” (e.g., group sizes/number randomized per condition; therapist guidance operationalization; randomization algorithm/sequence; exact VR scenario delivery per session). Finally, the rubric currently treats participant/material/procedure completeness somewhat collectively; you could clarify whether a single major omission (e.g., missing group sizes or intervention protocol definition) should cap the score more strongly.
results_content_summary: The results section reports a 2 (time: pre vs post) × 3 (condition: waitlist, self-led VR, therapist-led VR) mixed ANOVA approach and provides the key ANOVA test statistics, including the main effects and the time × condition interaction. It also attempts to follow with Holm-corrected post-hoc comparisons and describes whether each comparison matched the stated hypotheses. However, the section is incomplete and internally inconsistent: sample size is unclear (99 participants vs “Table 1” absent), outlier handling is vague, degrees of freedom appear to match a different N than stated, and multiple post-hoc p-values are formatted ambiguously (e.g., p = <.001). The absence of the actual descriptive table values and figure/table content makes the reporting difficult to evaluate against the described method.
results_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but contains numerous precision and formatting issues (e.g., typos like SVRET/TVRET, inconsistent naming, and p-value formatting such as “p = <.001” and missing decimals). Paragraph structure is mostly linear, but key results are missing because Table 1/Table 2 are not shown, and the figure is only named without content. APA compliance is weak in this snippet: tables/figures are referenced without providing the actual numbers, and statistical reporting is inconsistent (spacing and df patterns). Redundancy is minor, but clarity is reduced by ambiguous phrasing and inconsistent terminology.
results_rubric_feedback: The rubric could more explicitly distinguish “appropriate but incomplete reporting” from “incorrect statistics,” because here the ANOVA is plausible but the reporting is not fully verifiable due to missing tables/figures. The Results criteria would benefit from clearer requirements on whether descriptive tables (means/SDs), demographics, and figure content must be present in-text or can be omitted without heavily penalizing. Also, the rubric mentions “in-depth knowledge of statistical analyses,” but it does not provide concrete examples of what counts (e.g., correct df reporting, sphericity details, effect sizes like partial eta-squared, or specific assumptions checks). Finally, the band descriptors overlap (e.g., “mostly coherent and somewhat relevant” vs “mostly coherent and relevant”), so adding short decision rules (presence/absence of key elements, internal consistency checks) would make grading more consistent.
discussion_content_summary: The discussion attempts to answer the research question by stating that both VR conditions reduced SAD symptoms and that self-led VR (SVRET) outperformed therapist-led VR (TVRET). It briefly connects the findings to prior studies and proposes theoretical explanations using self-efficacy (Bandura) and a zone-of-proximal-development/interaction framing for therapist involvement. It includes multiple limitations (age range, lack of follow-up, and not directly testing the proposed mechanisms) and offers future research directions, including measuring fear of negative evaluation (FNE) and adding manipulation checks. However, key interpretation is not consistently grounded in the study’s actual hypothesis/results as presented, and the theoretical use (especially linking to what was and was not measured) is somewhat unclear or overstated.
discussion_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but contains frequent imprecision and incorrect wording (e.g., “SVRET/TVRET” inconsistencies, unclear phrasing like “works well as well,” and several grammar/tense issues). APA/statistical style is inconsistent: citations are sometimes missing proper author-year formatting and there are formatting irregularities (e.g., “Lindner et al, 2018” lacking consistent spacing; “Sources:” section lists several non-APA formatted items including websites). Paragraphing is uneven with very long paragraphs and minimal signposting, and some redundancy appears in re-stating effects and hypotheses. There are also issues with clarity/consistency in how measures and constructs are described (e.g., LSAS vs FNE rationale) and in the precision of theoretical claims.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion generally reflects an adequate attempt at interpretation, comparison to prior research, and critical reflection, which supports a developing-to-adequate band. To reach a higher band, the reasoning should be more tightly tied to the specific study design and what was actually measured (e.g., avoid claiming mechanism support when only outcomes were measured). The rubric would benefit from clearer, more observable thresholds distinguishing “nearly complete/somewhat relevant” from “relevant/convincingly argued” for study-specific limitations and future directions. It would also help if the rubric explicitly separated (a) correctness of the main conclusion vs (b) correctness/clarity of theory integration, since these often fail for different reasons.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style criteria would benefit from clearer, more objective thresholds for what counts as “different” APA errors vs. “vague/ambiguous” statements, because these are currently hard to calibrate consistently across graders. Adding brief examples for common categories (e.g., citation formatting, p-value formatting, table/figure referencing) would make the rubric easier to apply uniformly. The criterion currently mixes writing quality (structure/clarity) with formatting compliance; separating these into two sub-dimensions with independent descriptors could improve reliability and fairness.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides a reasonable starting point for the topic (SAD, adolescent relevance) and motivates the need for exposure-based treatments and more acceptable options like VRET. It also lays out a theoretical explanation of fear learning (classical/operant conditioning) and describes how exposure and VRET are expected to work. However, the theoretical framework is not clearly tied into a coherent, testable set of mechanisms that directly justify the final hypothesis comparison between VRET and IVET for adolescents. The previous-research section is largely descriptive and has some gaps in synthesis (e.g., what exactly is the key unresolved issue after Anderson/Kampmann/Bouchard), and the research question/hypotheses are only stated late and remain somewhat generic.
intro_style_notes: The language is mostly clear and readable, with generally correct grammar and spelling. There are APA issues such as using “APA, n.d.” instead of a proper in-text citation, inconsistent citation formatting (e.g., missing parentheses around some years, inconsistent “et al.” spacing), and at least one likely citation-year mismatch/incorrect reference detail (e.g., “Salari et al., 2024” for an estimated prevalence without clear grounding here). Paragraphing follows the broad structure, but there is some redundancy (e.g., repeated benefits of VRET) and a few imprecise or informal causal claims that would benefit from tighter academic wording.
intro_rubric_feedback: To improve against the rubric criteria, the introduction should more explicitly build a single line of argument culminating in a clear, researchable RQ (or at least a sharply specified aim) earlier, with hypotheses that are directly and logically derived from the theoretical framework and prior research. The theoretical framework should be used as an interpretive scaffold (constructs + stated relationships) rather than mainly as general conditioning/learning descriptions; ideally, you would state what about VRET vs IVET should change (e.g., perceived safety, exposure intensity/expectancy violation, mechanisms) and why that should differ specifically for adolescents. In the rubric’s sense, “previous research” should be synthesized into building blocks that directly justify the gap your RCT addresses (what is known, what is not, and why your design resolves it), rather than primarily summarizing individual outcomes and limitations. Finally, the hypotheses are currently testable but framed broadly; they should be tightened so the predicted direction and contrast map unambiguously onto the study design (VRET vs IVET vs waitlist) and the relevant constructs (SAD symptoms) introduced earlier.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section is broadly aligned with the stated RQ/hypothesis logic (comparing VRET vs IVET vs waitlist in SAD) and includes key elements: recruitment, inclusion/exclusion, allocation to conditions, main instrument (LSAS-CA), and a session overview. However, several methodological details required for replicability are missing or unclear, especially regarding exact demographics, group allocation procedure timing (e.g., whether stratification was used), therapist roles during VRET/IVET (e.g., frequency/standardization), and the waitlist duration/assessment schedule. Materials and Procedure also overlap somewhat (e.g., session content and tailoring described under Materials while the design should be anchored more cleanly in Procedure), and key design parameters are internally inconsistent with typical reporting (e.g., “10 sessions twice per week” vs “lasting 5 weeks”).
methods_style_notes: Language is generally clear, but there are numerous precision issues (e.g., unspecified ages despite calling them adolescents; unclear operationalization of therapist “tailoring” and how sessions map to the hierarchy). APA-wise, the section would benefit from consistent formatting of headings and removing some informal wording (e.g., “improper requests”) in favor of neutral scientific descriptions. Paragraph structure is mostly sensible (Participants/Materials/Procedure), but the Materials subsection is somewhat overloaded and repeats procedural detail. Redundancy appears between Materials and Procedure regarding exposure tailoring and therapist involvement.
methods_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s Methods bands are understandable, but the descriptors are still somewhat broad and can lead to different interpretations between graders (e.g., what counts as “somewhat comprehensibly” vs “comprehensibly” when crucial replication details are missing). Consider anchoring each band to concrete checklist items (e.g., demographics, allocation method, intervention length/timing, therapist fidelity/standardization, waitlist assessment timing) to reduce subjectivity. Also, “complete and correct” could be clearer by explicitly stating which subcomponents are mandatory for passing (participants, materials, procedure, analyses) and what level of detail is expected for each. Finally, the rubric mentions data analysis earlier but the Methods criterion currently does not explicitly require an “Analysis plan” subsection, which could be clarified since students often omit it.
results_content_summary: The Results section reports a mixed factorial ANOVA on LSAS-CA with clear reporting of main effects, the interaction, and Holm-corrected post-hoc comparisons at pre- and post-treatment. It includes an outlier-handling decision (two outliers at post-treatment) and describes assumption checking (Shapiro-Wilk normality violation for the waitlist at post; Levene’s test for homogeneity). The overall pattern is interpreted in line with some hypotheses (treatment vs waitlist) while also noting a non-significant treatment-vs-treatment comparison (IVET vs VRET) at post-treatment. However, several required quantitative details are missing (no means/SD values in Table 1/2, no effect sizes or test statistics for post-hocs, and the assumption-violation handling is not fully justified beyond citing the CLT).
results_style_notes: Language is mostly clear and appropriately scientific, with understandable paragraphing for the analysis flow. There are some APA/formatting and consistency issues: inconsistent naming of conditions (VRET vs VRET appears, and IVET/VRET abbreviations are not consistently introduced), a missing space and slight wording issues (e.g., “Levene’s test was met” without giving the test value; “N= 90”), and Table 2 content is not included in the provided text. References are embedded appropriately for the CLT, but statistical reporting could be formatted more consistently (e.g., p-value spacing and reporting exact statistics when claimed).
results_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s Results criteria are generally clear, but they could more explicitly anchor what “correct, complete” means for this course (e.g., expectation for descriptive tables with means/SDs, reporting of post-hoc statistics, and effect sizes). The category “Demonstrating an in depth knowledge of statistical analyses and reasoning” is somewhat vague; it would benefit from concrete indicators such as effect sizes, correction method transparency, and explicit handling of violated assumptions. The “mostly correct” vs “nearly complete” distinctions would be easier to apply if the rubric specified a minimum checklist of statistical elements expected at the student level. Finally, overlap between “relevant in terms of stated design and procedure” and “correct reporting” could be reduced by separating “alignment with design” (e.g., matching factor structure and time points) from “statistical correctness/completeness.”
discussion_content_summary: The discussion attempts to answer whether VRET is superior to IVET by reiterating that both active treatments reduced SAD symptoms more than the waitlist, while VRET did not outperform IVET at post-treatment. It provides some theoretical and study-comparison reasoning (conditioning/exposure rationale; references to prior VR trials) and explicitly proposes explanations for the null VRET vs IVET effect. However, parts of the interpretation are not fully consistent with how conclusions should follow from the presented results (e.g., wording suggests VRET/IVET patterns that are unclear), and the theoretical mechanisms introduced in the limitations do not always connect tightly to the study’s strongest findings. Limitations and future directions are present and relevant overall, but the critical reflection remains somewhat generic and sometimes relies on assumptions not tested in the study.
discussion_style_notes: Language is generally understandable, but there are precision problems (tense/subject-verb consistency, awkward phrasing like “analysed the effectiveness” and “as was hypothesized,” and some unclear causal statements). Paragraph structure roughly follows a discussion flow (summary → comparisons → limitations → future research → conclusion), but several paragraphs mix multiple ideas, reducing single-focus clarity. APA compliance is uneven in this section (e.g., inconsistent citation style and at least one incorrect/odd reference spelling in-text: “Lamb et al., 2005; Thorndike, 1898” with likely mismatched authorship), and there is some redundancy in restating results. Overall grammar and spelling are mostly acceptable, but several sentences reduce scientific polish.
discussion_rubric_feedback: Your rubric could be made more concrete by anchoring ‘critical reflection’ to observable criteria such as: at least two limitations must directly threaten internal validity/external validity of the specific design, and each must be connected to a specific pattern/result (e.g., null interaction, unexpected waitlist change). The ‘reasoning culminating in the main conclusion’ criterion would benefit from clearer sub-bands distinguishing (a) correct conclusion but weak mechanism/testing links versus (b) incorrect or unsupported conclusion. Some wording like “somewhat convincingly argued for” is subjective; adding anchors (e.g., use of testable mechanisms, explicit alternative explanations considered, and linkage to measures/manipulation) would improve reliability between graders.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s Language & Style bands are broadly helpful but still somewhat anchored to general impressions (e.g., “vague statements” or “excellent layout”) without concrete, observable indicators. It would benefit from clearer sub-criteria for APA mechanics (in-text citation consistency, reference list formatting, and statistical notation) versus prose quality (sentence-level clarity and signposting). Some descriptors overlap across bands (e.g., “some errors” vs “hardly any errors”), so adding small quantitative/locational anchors (e.g., “multiple incorrect in-text citations” or “major missing table/figure content”) would make the thresholds more reliable and less subjective.
final_grade_justification: Holistically, the paper shows an adequate overall fit to the RQ in that the study addresses VRET vs IVET for SAD with a waitlist control and uses an appropriate primary outcome (LSAS-CA) and a generally coherent ANOVA framework in the Results. However, key scientific-argument strengths are weakened by an insufficiently coherent, testable mechanism-based rationale in the Introduction and by missing/unclear methodological details that limit replicability (e.g., allocation procedure, therapist standardization, and assessment schedule). The Discussion mostly interprets the main treatment-vs-waitlist findings correctly, but it does not consistently or convincingly derive the central conclusion about VRET vs IVET from the presented statistics, and it lacks some depth in critical reflection. Language/style is broadly understandable, but the combination of reasoning and reporting gaps places the paper at the minimal passing band per the rubric.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides a clear societal and clinical motivation for treating adolescents with SAD, and it links exposure-based therapy to maintaining mechanisms using conditioning concepts. It also explains how VRET is expected to work and why adolescents might find it more acceptable than IVET, culminating in a plausible rationale for comparing VRET vs IVET. However, the theoretical framework is not used in a fully consistent way to derive the specific hypotheses/testable predictions; some claims are phrased broadly (“replacing response… proves falsity,” “VR allows in-depth manipulation”) without explicitly mapping mechanisms to the operationalized intervention features. The “previous research” part is present and generally relevant, but the transitions between studies are sometimes more descriptive than synthetic, and several citations used to support key assertions appear disconnected from the described argument (e.g., definitions and effect claims without showing their relevance to the adolescent SAD + VRET/IVET comparison). Overall, the research aim is stated, but the research question and hypotheses are somewhat implicit and could be more clearly formulated as a single, concise RQ/hypothesis set derived from the earlier argument.
intro_style_notes: Language is mostly understandable and the paragraph structure follows an intended progression (problem → treatment gap → theory → VRET rationale → previous research → study aim). There are several APA/compliance issues and inconsistencies (e.g., “APA, n.d.” for a clinical definition, inconsistent citation styles like “Ahrens et al. 2024” vs “Ahrens et al. 2024,” and mixed punctuation/abbreviation formatting such as IVET/IVET; “aspect found to predict” phrasing; typos like “exposed to the negative cognitions…,” and some awkward or ungrammatical constructions). The theoretical constructs are sometimes repeated with synonyms (e.g., fear/avoidant reinforcement, maladaptive associations, negative cognitions) without clear added specificity, creating redundancy. Signposting is present but could be improved with more explicit transitions (e.g., from conditioning theory → specific predictions for VRET vs IVET).
intro_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s Introduction criteria are generally appropriate (RQ clarity, relevance, coherence of the argument, hypothesis/testability, responsible referencing), but the bands would benefit from more concrete anchors distinguishing “somewhat coherent” from “coherently” and “convincingly argued for.” Criteria currently combine multiple constructs (RQ clarity, relevance, and argument quality) into one continuum, which makes it harder to diagnose specific weaknesses. Adding explicit checklist-like sub-criteria (e.g., “RQ explicitly stated,” “hypotheses explicitly derived from theory/previous research,” “synthetic linking between studies”) would reduce subjectivity. The rubric could also clarify how to judge hypotheses being “present but implicit” vs “present and testable,” and how to weigh occasional citation/argument mismatches compared to larger reasoning breaks.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section includes several core elements (participants, measures, intervention descriptions, and a rough procedure) and generally matches the stated RQ/hypotheses of comparing VRET vs IVET vs waitlist for SAD symptoms. However, the participant description contains major inconsistencies and incompleteness (age/“adolescents” vs no mean/SD or full demographics; APA year mismatch for DSM reference; and unclear whether “adolescents” are actually the target group operationally in the sample). The intervention description is detailed, but key methodological details needed for replication are missing or insufficiently specified (allocation concealment/blinding, session length totals, therapist-to-group implementation details, and the exact exposure stopping/termination rules). Finally, the procedure and timing are inconsistently reported (e.g., “10 sessions” over 5 weeks vs “two blocks of 30 minutes,” and no clear follow-up schedule), and the analysis plan is absent from the Methods (including which statistical tests correspond to the reported design).
methods_style_notes: Language is mostly clear but sometimes imprecise (“free treatment,” “until anxiety decreased” without operational criteria). There are several APA/consistency issues (DSM edition year cited as 2022 while “revised 5th edition” wording is used; variable/construct labels are clear but some wording is informal or vague). Paragraphing follows the standard headings, but there is redundancy between materials and procedure for certain details (session structure and exposure progression). Overall APA compliance for Methods (citations/layout) is acceptable at a basic level, though the text lacks key structured reporting components typical for this course and for replicability.
methods_rubric_feedback: Several rubric criteria could be more concretely anchored to observable reporting requirements for PT:PR (e.g., a checklist-like “must include” list for inclusion/exclusion, allocation, timing, and planned analyses). The rubric bands for Introduction and Discussion are relatively qualitative, but Methods and Results would benefit from clearer “minimum evidence” definitions (e.g., whether missing an analysis plan should cap the Methods/Results score at a specific level). The rubric currently mixes conceptual coherence with completeness; splitting these into separate sub-criteria would reduce subjectivity. Finally, the rubric does not explicitly weight common “fatal omissions” in Methods (e.g., missing analysis plan or missing timing), which can disproportionately affect whether a paper would be replicable for a bachelor thesis.
results_content_summary: The section reports a mixed ANOVA with two time points and three conditions on LSAS-CA, includes outlier handling via boxplots, and presents descriptive statistics tables (Table 1 and Table 2) and a figure (Figure 1). It reports key omnibus effects (main effect of time, non-significant condition main effect, and a significant time × condition interaction) and follows with Holm-corrected post-hoc comparisons at pre- and post-treatment. However, the reporting is incomplete/inconsistent with the presented methodology: it uses LSAS-CA yet earlier methods/results context appears to suggest LSAS-SR/other measures; it also reports the outlier numbers but does not provide the underlying data handling decision details (e.g., influence, robustness, or justification for retaining). Finally, the statistical reporting lacks important elements (e.g., effect sizes, degrees of freedom consistency checks, and assumptions around normality violations despite proceeding with the central limit theorem) and is a bit unclear about how exactly the post-hoc tests map onto the interaction.
results_style_notes: Language is generally understandable and mostly uses appropriate scientific phrasing, but there are several imprecise or awkward constructions (e.g., “Their values still fit the scale,” “matched the expectations… however”) that could be tightened. APA formatting is inconsistently applied (e.g., Table captions/headers, spacing, and capitalization of scale/variables such as LSAS-CA vs LSAS-CA scores). The Results paragraphs are mostly logically ordered, but there is redundancy and some missing specificity (e.g., no mention of sample means/SDs in text, no effect sizes), which affects clarity more than grammar. There is also minor punctuation/typography inconsistency (e.g., “p=.004” vs “p < .001,” inconsistent spacing in df values like “N= 90”).
results_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s “Results” criterion is broadly framed (correct/complete/coherent/relevant), but it does not explicitly specify which quantitative anchors are required for an “adequate/good” band (e.g., effect sizes, df consistency, assumption handling details, reporting of key descriptives and test statistics). The descriptor for “in-depth knowledge of statistical analyses” risks subjectivity because it’s unclear what threshold of stats knowledge (beyond significance tests) should be demonstrated at bachelor level. Adding concrete checklists—such as whether omnibus effects, interaction, relevant follow-ups, assumption checks, and effect sizes are reported—would make the grading bands more reliable. Also, the rubric could clarify how to judge when reported analyses are “mostly correct” but mismatch the methods (e.g., instrument name/scale) since this is a major replication-validity issue.
discussion_content_summary: The discussion states a clear main conclusion: VRET and IVET both reduced adolescents’ SAD symptoms, but VRET was not more effective than IVET at post-treatment. The author connects expected and unexpected findings to prior literature and offers a mechanistic explanation (cognitive avoidance and the role of CBT) for why VRET might not outperform IVET. Several limitations and future directions are provided, including realism of VR dialogue structure and potential differences in therapeutic alliance. However, there are substantial problems with internal consistency and argument precision (e.g., the introduction-level claim of “VRET vs IVET” vs multiple earlier statements about waitlist and “SAD symptoms decreased significantly” without careful framing; also some cited support is not tightly matched to the described mechanism).
discussion_style_notes: The section is generally readable and uses mostly appropriate scientific tone, but there are multiple grammatical and phrasing issues (e.g., tense/number agreement, awkward constructions like “as was hypothesized” without precise mapping to the reported statistics, and “decrease of symptoms… supported by previous research”). APA compliance appears inconsistent in places: abbreviations and capitalization are inconsistent (SAD vs “SAD symptoms”; IVET/VRET usage), citations are sometimes missing commas/format consistency, and there are a few problematic reference entries in the provided text (e.g., use of “et al.” patterns is inconsistent across the manuscript). Paragraphing follows the expected discussion flow (results → theory → limitations → future research → conclusion), but redundancy and imprecise causal language reduce clarity.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The rubric could more explicitly distinguish between (a) correctly answering the RQ/main conclusion and (b) correctly interpreting and integrating the theoretical framework and prior findings. Some criteria are still quite broad (e.g., “convincingly argued for” and “relevant critical reflection”), which makes grading subjective; adding observable sub-anchors (e.g., “at least two findings compared to prior results with explicit ‘why’,” “limitations are design-specific and tie to interpretation of at least one key result”) would improve reliability. The discussion bands would benefit from clearer separation between “mentions limitations” vs “links limitations to alternative interpretations and effect on the main conclusion.” Finally, the rubric could explicitly penalize internal inconsistency (e.g., claiming a hypothesis was confirmed/disconfirmed while the argument elsewhere contradicts itself) as a separate descriptor.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style bands could be anchored more concretely by specifying what counts as “numerous” vs. “few” APA/layout errors (e.g., number of citation formatting errors, missing headings, or table inconsistencies per page). Some descriptors overlap with scientific structure (e.g., “single focus”) and could be separated more clearly from language/APA mechanics to reduce subjectivity. The rubric would benefit from clearer thresholds for “vague or ambiguous statements” (examples or categories like incorrect tense, unclear referents, or causal language). Finally, adding a short checklist per band (e.g., “0–1 APA issues” vs “2–5 APA issues”) would make grading more consistent across graders.
final_grade_justification: Holistically, the paper does not yet meet the core requirements for a credible scientific article in its current form, mainly due to substantial internal inconsistencies across Introduction, Methods, and Results (e.g., mismatch/ambiguity of target sample details and unclear timing/design reporting), and missing elements of a defensible analysis plan. While the Results and Discussion contain some correct elements and an overall plausible conclusion, the scientific argument does not coherently and operationally connect the theoretical mechanism to specific intervention features and testable hypotheses, and the statistical reporting lacks essential details (e.g., effect sizes, consistency checks, clear mapping to the interaction). Because these issues would likely prevent the student from achieving a passing standard for a next-year bachelor thesis-level paper, the appropriate holistic outcome is a fail per the rubric’s overall criterion emphasis on scientific reasoning and method/result alignment.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides a clear general topic and builds societal relevance for adolescents with SAD, including why exposure-based treatment matters and why alternatives like VRET may be appealing. It also sketches a theoretical rationale (conditioning mechanisms, operant reinforcement) and links exposure principles to VRET, but the theoretical pathway to the specific research question is partly diffuse. The “previous research” section includes multiple studies and highlights gaps (adult-focused evidence and limited adolescent comparisons), yet the literature synthesis and argumentation do not fully culminate in a crisp, well-justified research question and hypotheses derived from the theory. The hypotheses are stated and testable in a general way, but the transition to the study design is somewhat abrupt and not strongly grounded in a precise mechanistic expectation for VRET vs IVET in adolescents.
intro_style_notes: Language is generally understandable with mostly correct grammar, but there are several imprecise wordings and capitalization issues (e.g., “APA, n.d.”; IVET abbreviation consistency; “aspect found to predict” without clear sentence structure). There are multiple APA-related concerns for an introduction draft, such as inconsistent reference formatting and occasional unclear parenthetical citations (e.g., “Ahrens et al. 2024” lacking punctuation, “Ahrens et al. 2024” vs “Ahrens et al. 2024”). Paragraphing is mostly logical, but there is redundancy and long sentences that reduce clarity. Overall APA style cannot be considered “compliant” yet, but it is close enough to be readable and assessable.
intro_rubric_feedback: To improve alignment with the rubric, the introduction would benefit from making the line of reasoning culminating in the RQ/hypotheses more explicit and tightly connected to the theoretical framework and prior research. As written, key constructs are defined, but the mechanism linking (i) adolescents’ characteristics, (ii) VRET’s properties, and (iii) the expected differential effect versus IVET is not argued in a sufficiently structured, step-by-step way. The “previous research” section summarizes several studies, but the synthesis does not consistently build towards the specific gap with a clear “therefore we test X” logic; this weakens the convincingly-argued RQ and hypothesis component. Finally, the hypotheses are testable, but they are somewhat generic (all decrease; VRET > IVET) rather than sharply derived from the specific theoretical and empirical shortcomings discussed.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section describes a coherent randomized three-arm design (VRET, IVET, waitlist) with clear participant targeting (adolescents with SAD) and reasonably specified inclusion/exclusion criteria. Materials and procedure are generally aligned with the stated research aim of comparing VRET and IVET, including basic details of intervention structure (session number/frequency, hierarchy creation, and exposure progression) and measurement using LSAS-CA. However, key methodological details are missing or vague for replication and scientific evaluation (e.g., demographics reporting, compensation, attrition handling, exact timing of assessment points beyond pre/post, adherence/intensity criteria, and how randomization and treatment fidelity were ensured/monitored). Several claims are also hard to evaluate because terminology is sometimes imprecise (e.g., “adolescents” without age range; “score of 22.5 represents the best cut-off” without specifying the validation context).
methods_style_notes: Language is mostly clear and formal, with few grammar issues. APA-style referencing is used, but there are some inconsistencies such as introducing tools/constructs without consistent level of specificity and occasional unclear phrasing (e.g., “They experienced every virtual world at least once, and until their anxiety decreased.”). Paragraph structure generally follows the expected Methods components, but the Materials section mixes independent-variable/intervention implementation details with insufficient separation from procedure details. Overall, redundancy is low, but precision is sometimes insufficient for scientific replication.
methods_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s Methods criterion is fairly solid in distinguishing “coherent/aligned and complete/correct” from “incomplete/incomprehensible,” which matches how graders should judge replicability. However, the band descriptors (Adequate→Good→Excellent) rely on relatively subjective judgments about “somewhat comprehensibly” and “described comprehensibly,” without concrete anchors for what must be present (e.g., minimum required timing points, randomization procedure details, adherence/fidelity measures). Adding a checklist-like set of concrete anchors under the rubric (while keeping the four bands) would reduce inconsistency between graders. Finally, the rubric conflates “participants/materials/procedures described” with “study design coherence”; splitting these into two sub-criteria (design coherence vs. replicability/completeness) would make scoring more transparent.
results_content_summary: The results describe a coherent 3 (condition) × 2 (time) mixed ANOVA on LSAS-CA, including sample size, outlier handling, key assumption checks (Shapiro-Wilk for normality and Levene’s for homogeneity), main effects, and an interaction. The section also reports post-hoc comparisons with Holm correction across pre- and post-treatment, and it links findings to the stated hypotheses (including noting a null difference between IVET and VRET at post). However, several statistical and reporting details are incomplete or slightly inconsistent for replication and evaluation: the exact degrees of freedom/ANOVA structure is not fully consistent, the reporting of outlier inclusion is somewhat under-justified, and Figure 1 is not summarized with actual pattern values or statistics. Overall, the main inferential claims appear plausible and mostly correctly framed, but the rigor and completeness are not at “good/excellent” level.
results_style_notes: The section is mostly clear and uses appropriate scientific phrasing, with tables and an explicit figure reference. There are a few precision issues (e.g., “two outliers… included in the analysis” is stated, but justification/criteria for inclusion is not detailed) and some minor APA inconsistencies (e.g., missing italicization/format consistency in headings, inconsistent use of abbreviation spacing, and “values … still fit the scale” phrasing that is not standard). Paragraph transitions are generally fine, but there is some redundancy (e.g., describing multiple pairwise comparisons in-line without a compact reporting format). Grammar is largely correct, with minor punctuation/spacing inconsistencies.
results_rubric_feedback: Clarify what level of “incompleteness” in assumption reporting should lower the Results score (e.g., should non-normality trigger alternative analyses, and is that expected to be mentioned explicitly?). The rubric bands would benefit from more concrete anchors about statistical reporting completeness: for instance, whether effect sizes (partial eta-squared) and exact post-hoc comparisons structure are required to reach “good” vs “excellent.” Also, the rubric’s “demonstrating an in depth knowledge of statistical analyses and reasoning” is currently broad; adding specific indicators (effect sizes, multiple comparison correction clarity, consistency between df and design, and coherence between figure/table claims and reported tests) would reduce subjectivity.
discussion_content_summary: The discussion addresses the main research question by concluding that both VRET and IVET reduce SAD symptoms, but VRET is not superior to IVET at post-treatment. The student attempts to interpret unexpected null differences with an account involving cognitive avoidance and differences in how exposure is experienced in VR versus in vivo. The section also provides two study-specific limitations (dialogue realism/uncertainty targeting and therapeutic alliance) and offers concrete future research directions (more interactive avatar dialogues, measuring alliance, comparing VRET vs VRET+CBT). However, the discussion shows several inconsistencies with the stated results/hypotheses and some interpretations rely on assumptions rather than directly linking to the study’s actual measurements and mechanisms.
discussion_style_notes: The language is generally clear but contains imprecise wording and multiple grammar/structure issues (e.g., “will be”/tense inconsistencies, “analyze” phrasing, some awkward causal sentences). Paragraph structure mostly follows a discussion logic (results summary → comparison → limitations → future research → conclusion), but some paragraphs mix multiple claims (e.g., aligning with theory while also making new inferences). APA/Reference formatting is uneven (e.g., references list contains unrelated/uncited items from earlier content, and several citations appear for claims not fully tied to the study). There is some redundancy and occasional vague phrasing (“emphasize,” “supported by,” “truth-value”), and the conceptual terms are sometimes introduced without tight integration to the study’s operationalization.
discussion_rubric_feedback: Strengths: the discussion provides a coherent overall answer to the research question, distinguishes expected vs unexpected findings, and includes more than generic limitations with plausible mechanism-based future work. Improvements needed for a higher score: (1) make the link between results and theoretical mechanisms more evidence-grounded and consistent with the introduction/hypotheses (avoid adding new assumptions that the study did not test); (2) clearly separate “what the data show” from “possible explanations,” and ensure each limitation/future direction directly follows from the study’s design and measured constructs; (3) tighten references so that every cited study clearly supports a specific claim you make in that sentence/paragraph. Finally, ensure terminology and logic are consistent (e.g., correctly stating what was found at post-treatment and how that affects the hypothesis) and reduce mixed-claim paragraphs to keep single-focus topicality.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: To improve consistency, the Language & Style rubric should clarify what counts as “minor” versus “numerous” APA/referencing errors with concrete examples (e.g., missing italics, inconsistent reference formatting, incorrect in-text citation punctuation). The band descriptors partly overlap across levels (e.g., “some vague or ambiguous statements” vs “few vague or ambiguous statements”); adding a more operational definition (number of occurrences per page/section) would reduce subjectivity. It could also separate style quality (e.g., scientific tone, paragraphing) from APA mechanics (format/layout), because they tend to vary independently. Finally, including one clear anchor statement per band (e.g., “Good: readable with occasional APA slips, no disruption to interpretation”) would make grading more reliable.
final_grade_justification: Overall, the paper shows a coherent study concept, an analysis that broadly matches the stated design (mixed ANOVA with appropriate general framing), and conclusions that correctly reflect the presence of improvements across conditions and the lack of a clear VRET-superiority effect at post. However, the introduction only partly forges a precise mechanistic bridge from theory to the specific prediction about VRET vs IVET in adolescents, and the discussion contains several interpretive inconsistencies relative to what was actually measured. Methodological reporting is not sufficiently complete for replication (e.g., randomization/treatment fidelity, key assessment timing, adherence criteria), and results reporting lacks some precision and clarity. Language/style is generally understandable, but the scientific reasoning and reporting gaps keep the paper at the minimum passing band rather than a solid “good” level.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides a relevant clinical rationale by describing SAD, its prevalence/onset in adolescence, and the treatment gap for exposure-based CBT. It then offers a theoretical narrative (classical/operant learning principles) and connects those mechanisms to exposure therapy and VRET, with several plausible advantages of VR for adolescents. However, the theoretical framework is not clearly tied to a specific, testable set of constructs, and the “line of reasoning” becomes somewhat descriptive rather than argumentatively scaffolded toward the research question and hypothesis. The prior research discussion does identify comparisons relevant to VRET vs IVET, but the final transition to the current study’s unique contribution and hypotheses is still somewhat under-argued and the research question is largely implicit rather than clearly stated.
intro_style_notes: Language is generally understandable and uses mostly scientific phrasing, but there are noticeable grammar/wording issues (e.g., “classical conditioning” sentence structure, phrasing like “exposed to real-life” missing articles, occasional awkward constructions). APA compliance is weak in places: sources are cited as “APA, n.d.” without clear author/year formatting, and “Leigh & Clark, 2018” etc. are used but the reference style appears inconsistent; also there are at least one citation formatting inconsistencies (e.g., “Ahrens et al 2024” without comma, “aspect found to predict…”). Paragraphing is present but some paragraphs have multiple ideas stacked together, and redundancy appears in the mechanism/benefit explanations without tightening to the RQ.
intro_rubric_feedback: 1) The rubric criteria for “RQ clarity + culmination in relevance and hypothesis” would benefit from more concrete anchors: e.g., explicitly require an overt RQ sentence (“Therefore, we ask whether…”) and a clearly stated hypothesis with independent/dependent variables. 2) The band descriptors currently emphasize “coherence” and “convincingly argued for,” which can be subjective; adding a checklist-based component (e.g., theory→constructs→mechanism→prediction) would make scoring more reliable. 3) The rubric could better distinguish between “missing RQ statement” and “RQ present but weakly justified,” because these are qualitatively different failure modes for a first-year paper.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section describes a coherent randomized controlled design comparing VRET, IVET, and a waitlist, and it includes relevant participant eligibility/exclusion criteria, an identified primary outcome (LSAS-CA), and basic treatment structure (10 sessions over 5 weeks; 2× per week). However, important methodological details are missing or imprecise for a study at this level: key aspects of allocation concealment/blinding, exact inclusion criteria (e.g., diagnostic threshold on LSAS-CA/SCID details), and comprehensive intervention protocol standardization are not fully specified. The procedure section is fairly narrative and includes some administration details, but it lacks clarity on timing of measurements beyond pre/post, therapist-to-condition equivalence, and what “waitlist” specifically entailed before crossover. Overall, the study design is directionally appropriate for the stated comparison, but replicability is limited by insufficient operational detail.
methods_style_notes: The language is mostly clear and uses appropriate scientific terminology. There are some imprecisions and grammatical issues (e.g., “setup comprised of,” “comprised of three computers,” and occasional awkward phrasing like “The possible virtual scenarios included: … adopted from …”). APA compliance is mixed: citations are present in-text, but the Methods structure could be made more consistent (e.g., clearer subheadings for Participants/Materials/Procedure/Analyses) and it uses some procedural/administrative narration that would benefit from tighter, more objective phrasing. Paragraphing is generally logical, but there is some redundancy between Materials and Procedure (e.g., treatment duration/session blocks described in both places).
methods_rubric_feedback: The rubric would benefit from clearer, more concrete anchors for what counts as “complete and correct” methods details at bachelor level—especially for Participants (diagnostic assessment method and thresholds), Materials (full operationalization of interventions/controls), and Procedure (timing of measurement points, adherence monitoring, and crossover/waitlist specifics). The bands currently rely somewhat on subjective judgments (e.g., “somewhat comprehensibly described”), so adding checklisted sub-elements (allocation method, inclusion/exclusion thresholds, intervention fidelity/adherence, assessment schedule, crossover handling) would reduce ambiguity. Finally, it may help to explicitly separate “design coherence” from “replicability completeness,” since a study can be directionally coherent but still miss key replication-critical elements.
results_content_summary: The Results section reports an appropriate basic mixed ANOVA for a 3 (condition) × 2 (time) design using LSAS-CA and includes key elements such as sample size, outlier inspection, assumption checks (Shapiro-Wilk and Levene’s), and main effects/interactions. It clearly reports which pairwise differences were significant using Holm-corrected post-hoc tests and links the pattern to the stated hypotheses, including the non-significant IVET vs. VRET contrast. However, several statistical details are incomplete/unclear (e.g., the normality violation is acknowledged but the analysis decision is justified mainly via CLT without discussing how this affects validity for ANOVA; effect sizes are absent; and Figure 1 is referenced but not provided here). The reporting is mostly coherent and relevant to the stated design, but it falls short of the “complete and correct” band due to missing quantitative descriptive results (Table 1/Table 2 values not shown), limited transparency about outlier handling, and some inconsistencies (e.g., including “still fit the scale” as justification).
results_style_notes: Language is generally clear and mostly scientific, with appropriate use of statistical terminology and parentheses for df reporting. There are a few grammar/formatting issues (e.g., “Boxplots … revealed no outliers, while … contained two outliers” is fine, but “Their values … still fit the scale” is somewhat informal; capitalization inconsistencies like “Per condition” vs. “Per condition, the …”). APA/statistical formatting needs tightening: Table captions are incomplete (no actual values shown), and the section lacks effect sizes and consistent reporting of degrees of freedom/significant thresholds throughout. Paragraphing is mostly structured, but some sentences are long and contain multiple claims without clear separation.
results_rubric_feedback:
The Results section is largely aligned with the described design and reports the main inferential test and relevant post-hoc comparisons, which fits the rubric’s “mostly correct/mostly relevant” zone. To reach a higher band, the section would need more complete reporting of the descriptive statistics (actual Table 1/Table 2 values), more transparent handling/justification of outliers beyond inclusion, and stronger statistical reporting (e.g., effect sizes and clearer decision logic when normality is violated). The post-hoc strategy is conceptually appropriate, but further clarity about what exactly was compared (and where Holm correction applies) would make the reporting closer to “complete and coherent.”

Rubric-design feedback: The Results criterion conflates multiple dimensions (correctness of stats, completeness of reporting, coherence, and demonstration of in-depth statistical knowledge) without specifying concrete “must-have” items (e.g., effect sizes, correction scope, df format consistency). The descriptors are fairly subjective (“mostly coherent”, “somewhat relevant”), so adding checkable anchors (e.g., “reports means/SDs per cell,” “reports at least partial eta-squared/omega-squared,” “states post-hoc comparison structure”) would improve reliability between graders. The rubric would also benefit from separating “statistical appropriateness” from “reporting completeness,” since a student can choose the right test but underreport essentials (or vice versa).
discussion_content_summary: The discussion restates the main pattern that IVET and VRET both reduce SAD symptoms relative to baseline, but VRET is not superior to IVET at post-treatment. It makes an effort to connect findings to hypotheses, theoretical mechanisms (conditioning, overgeneralization, cognitive avoidance), and cites limitations (VR dialogue realism via semi-structured interactions; therapeutic alliance differences). It also proposes specific future research adjustments (more interactive VR dialogue; measuring alliance; comparing VRET vs VRET+CBT). However, several interpretations are weakly grounded in the presented results and sometimes do not clearly account for key design specifics (e.g., adolescent outcomes, exact constructs measured, and why the proposed mechanism would yield null VRET>IVET effects).
discussion_style_notes: Language is generally understandable and scientific, but there are frequent imprecise or incorrect phrases (e.g., “analysed the effectiveness … compared … in adolescents” and tense/grammar issues like “the expectation that VRET will be superior”).
