APA/statistical and reference formatting is uneven: the section includes an informal conclusion and a “Reference List” pasted inside the discussion text, with inconsistent citation quality and some references that appear unrelated to claims. Paragraphing is present but some paragraphs mix multiple topics (finding summary, explanation, literature comparison, then limitations), weakening the single-focus structure expected in this course. There is also some redundancy and informal phrasing (e.g., “quite stable”, “strangely”, “overall…”) and a few unclear sentences.
discussion_rubric_feedback: To strengthen the rubric itself, clarify the boundary between “mostly correct/relevant” interpretation vs. “wishful thinking/speculation” by adding anchor examples (e.g., when an interpretation is grounded in a specific result pattern). The Discussion criteria could benefit from more concrete indicators of “connect to theory/literature” (e.g., explicit requirement of at least two direct links to the introduction’s specific theoretical mechanisms or constructs). Finally, the language/style band descriptors could be made less subjective by separating APA/reference-list placement issues from general grammar clarity, so graders don’t have to infer the same underlying construct from different superficial problems.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric would benefit from clearer, more operational anchors distinguishing “some errors” vs “numerous errors,” especially for APA referencing and statistical formatting. Several bands mix multiple sub-skills (structure, grammar, APA, vagueness, redundancy) without specifying how each weighs into the final style judgment, making it potentially subjective. Adding concrete examples (e.g., what counts as an “APA layout error” or “vague statement”) and tightening the descriptors for the “Adequate/Good/Excellent” transitions would improve reliability between graders.
final_grade_justification: Although the Methods and Results are broadly consistent with a two-condition VRET design, critical replicability and operationalization details are missing (especially guidance content/dosing, diagnostic thresholds, and procedural timing), which undermines scientific rigor. The Introduction provides some rationale but the theoretical line of reasoning to the research question and hypothesis is not sufficiently coherent or fully specified for expected trajectories. The Results section contains reporting/consistency problems (e.g., unclear/absent descriptive statistics and internal inconsistencies in sample size), limiting confidence in the statistical conclusions. Overall, the paper’s weaknesses in scientific reasoning, reporting completeness, and replicability are substantial enough that it is unlikely to reach a passing standard for a bachelor-level thesis next year without major revision.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides a general rationale for studying social anxiety disorder and motivates VR exposure as a feasible alternative to in vivo exposure. It also reviews relevant prior research on (therapist-guided) VRET and briefly connects the gap to the need to compare therapist-guided vs self-guided VRET. However, the theoretical reasoning is partly inconsistent (CBT described alongside extinction/pavlovian framing without a clear integration into a testable mechanism for guidance), and the research gap/punchline becomes clear but the study’s research question and hypotheses are not fully specified and operationally aligned with the described results design. The final hypothesis is only partially testable/precise (e.g., post-treatment only, no clear role of waitlist/trajectories vs follow-up, and no clear definition of “greater reductions” or how it will be analyzed).
intro_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but includes several precision/grammar issues (e.g., “selfguided,” “RTC,” “Goetter,” inconsistent punctuation/spaces, “Kindred et al.. 2022,” and some awkward phrasing). APA-style consistency is weak in places (double dots, inconsistent capitalization of abbreviations like VRET/TG-VRET, and some reference/citation formatting issues). Paragraphing is mostly logical, but transitions are sometimes abrupt and the introduction contains some redundancy (multiple broad statements about prevalence and treatment motivation without tightening to the specific RQ).
intro_rubric_feedback: Clarify the hourglass-style line of reasoning: after introducing CBT/exposure theory, the paper needs a tighter, consistent theoretical framework that directly explains why therapist guidance should (or should not) change symptom reductions relative to self-guidance. Make the research question explicit in one sentence and ensure hypotheses are fully testable, specify the comparison(s) (including time points) and the direction(s) for all relevant outcomes. The prior research section should more clearly synthesize what each study adds toward the guidance vs self-guidance mechanism (adherence, feedback, expectancy violation, safety behaviors), rather than summarizing results in a mostly sequential way. Finally, ensure the final stated hypothesis matches the actual design described (pre/post/follow-up and how “reductions” will be quantified), so the reader sees a coherent link from theory → gap → RQ → hypotheses.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section includes core elements (participants, materials, procedure) and provides some demographics and randomization/exclusion details. However, it is not sufficiently complete or precise to allow replication of the study as described in the introduction: the design appears to be only two conditions (n=60 total) but the study aims/hypotheses in the paper concern a waitlist control as well, and group allocation/condition numbers are unclear relative to the stated design. Several key method details are missing or underspecified (e.g., therapist guidance specifics, VR content/scenario structure, session protocol, adherence/compliance monitoring, and whether/how LSAS-SR cutoffs/DSM diagnosis were operationalized). Overall, the description is coherent at a high level but contains important conceptual and procedural gaps that prevent judging the methodological quality as “complete and correct.”
methods_style_notes: Language is mostly understandable but contains multiple precision issues (e.g., unclear condition logic like “built-in virtual therapist” vs “real therapist”, “participants take home” vs “use during the session with the therapist”). There are several grammar/wording problems (articles and agreement errors, run-on sentences, and some inconsistent phrasing such as “asks how much fear or avoidance a person would feel”). APA compliance is only partial: citations are present, but reference formatting is inconsistent (and DSM/diagnostic wording is imprecise). Paragraphing into subheadings is clear, but content is sometimes repetitive or vague, reducing clarity.
methods_rubric_feedback: The rubric for Methods is currently somewhat broad about what counts as “complete and correct,” but it leaves room for subjective judgment on how much missing detail is fatal. Consider adding concrete required anchors for this course’s typical replication standard (e.g., IV operationalization: number and type of scenarios, session duration, therapist involvement specifics; DV measurement timing; and how diagnosis/inclusion thresholds are applied). Also, it may help to explicitly weight “design alignment” (e.g., number of conditions vs stated hypotheses) separately from “description completeness,” because conceptual mismatches can warrant a lower band than minor omissions.
results_content_summary: The results section reports a mixed-design ANOVA with main effects of time and condition plus a Time × Condition interaction, and it provides Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons that generally match the stated pattern of greater improvement for therapist-guided at post-treatment. However, the section is missing essential descriptive elements (e.g., the actual Table with cell means/SDs, participant-by-condition Ns across time, and a figure/graph), which prevents checking coherence with the analyses. Assumption checking is described only in general terms and outlier handling is mentioned, but without a clear criterion or whether outliers affect ANOVA assumptions. Overall, the reporting is too incomplete and internally inconsistent for the methods/design as described earlier.
results_style_notes: Language is mostly comprehensible, but several sentences are vague or grammatically flawed (e.g., “the research has decided…”; “At baseline…lower mean scores at post-treatment and follow-up” without numbers). There are APA/statistical reporting issues: degrees of freedom suggest an ANOVA setup inconsistent with the stated N=60 and the two-condition structure (but DF/within-subject dfs are not reconciled), and effect sizes/terms are inconsistently formatted. The section also contains incomplete table labeling (“Average scores on x”) and lacks clear separation of condition/time-specific reporting. Paragraphing is somewhat clear (headings present) but the logical flow is interrupted by missing numerical outputs and absent tables/figures.
results_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s Results criteria could better separate (a) completeness of required elements for this course (tables by condition × time, demographics table, and plot) from (b) correctness/appropriateness of statistical reporting. Band descriptors (e.g., “mostly correct/complete”) would benefit from more concrete anchors like: ‘includes descriptive Table(s) and figure’ and ‘reports exact F/df/p for all tested effects and planned post-hocs’ to reduce subjectivity. The rubric would also improve by explicitly addressing internal consistency between the described design in Methods and the analyses reported in Results (e.g., matching number of conditions, factor definitions, and degrees of freedom). Finally, outlier handling and assumption checks could be given clearer expectations (criterion + how handled) to make grading more consistent.
discussion_content_summary: The discussion restates the study aim and provides an interpretation consistent with the reported pattern: both conditions improved, therapist-guided more strongly immediately, and effects converge by follow-up. It offers a theoretical explanation (self-efficacy) for the unexpected continuation of improvement in the self-guided group and connects findings to prior VRET trials. The section also includes multiple limitations (response bias due to different survey context, generalizability to young university samples, context-dependent exposure), and it proposes future directions that follow from these points. However, the discussion sometimes introduces claims that are not clearly supported by the presented data (e.g., “benefits…stable” and details about follow-up comparisons), and engagement with the exact research question/hypotheses and statistical results is not fully precise.
discussion_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but contains grammar errors (e.g., missing/incorrect articles and phrasing like “would continue improving beyond post-treatment,” “Could potentially be explained due the presence of a therapist being available,” “differences could be explained between conditions”). APA/statistical precision is weak in places: the text mentions outcomes (immediate measurability, stability, convergence) without clear linkage to the specific analyses/p-values/figures, and there are reference formatting issues (the reference list is included, with several inconsistencies and even stray duplicated text near the end). Paragraphing is mostly logical, but there is redundancy and some unclear transitions (e.g., mixing implications and limitations, and “Thirdly,” while earlier limitations are already listed).
discussion_rubric_feedback: Your discussion includes the required core elements: a main conclusion tied to the aim, comparison to prior research, critical limitations, and concrete future research ideas. To score higher on the rubric, the reasoning needs to be more tightly anchored to the actual reported results (e.g., explicitly describing what “stable” and “comparable” mean in terms of the follow-up pattern and significance) and to the stated hypotheses from the introduction. Additionally, some claims are speculative or framed too strongly without clear justification from the results, and the theoretical explanations should be linked more directly to constructs and to what your design actually tests. Finally, improve APA discipline and clarity in this section by removing irrelevant artifacts, tightening sentences with grammar/precision, and ensuring all stated comparisons are traceable to the results.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric bands could be made more concrete by anchoring them to observable indicators (e.g., number of APA formatting errors, clarity of paragraph/topic sentences, frequency of vague statements). Some descriptors (“graceful style”, “near faultless”, “some redundancy”) are still somewhat subjective and would benefit from clearer operational thresholds or examples. The rubric also mixes language accuracy and structural coherence without specifying how heavily each should weigh within the same band. Adding clearer gradations for how minor vs. major APA/statistical formatting issues affect the score would improve consistency between graders.
final_grade_justification: Although the introduction and discussion show awareness of the relevant topic and provide a plausible interpretive narrative, the paper’s central scientific requirements are not met for a coherent, replicable study. The Methods section is too underspecified and internally misaligned with the stated design (e.g., waitlist/control elements unclear), and the Results section is missing essential descriptive components (e.g., no cell means/SDs, Ns, or figure), preventing verification of the reported analyses. The discussion includes some relevant limitations but also makes or implies claims that are not clearly supported by the incomplete results reporting. Given these major gaps in methodological transparency and evidence reporting, the paper falls below the “adequate” band overall and would not reliably support the competence expected for a passing bachelor-thesis-level writing task next year.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides relevant background on SAD, outlines why exposure-based treatment (and VR in particular) may matter, and it mentions several key prior studies on VRET. However, the theoretical line of reasoning is not clearly built into a coherent framework that logically culminates in a specific, testable research question and hypothesis. The prior research section is mostly a descriptive summary of studies, with weaker synthesis (what each study adds to the argument toward guided vs self-guided VRET). The stated hypothesis is testable, but the introduction leaves key elements under-specified (e.g., the exact research question in terms of comparisons/timepoints, and how theory predicts the pattern at post vs follow-up).
intro_style_notes: Language is generally readable but includes grammatical and precision issues (e.g., inconsistent punctuation, misspellings like “Selfguided-VRET/selfguided-VRET,” and incorrect or imprecise phrasing such as “Pavlovian extinction model” explanation). Several references appear with formatting inconsistencies (e.g., “Kindred et al.. 2022,” “Kampmann et al. 2015/2016” inconsistency with required core set), and some citations seem not fully supported by the specific claims. Paragraph structure loosely follows a narrative flow, but topical sentences and transitions between therapy-theory-prior research-design are sometimes unclear, and there is some redundancy (e.g., repeating “effective treatment” ideas without adding new argument steps).
intro_rubric_feedback: Several rubric elements are met partially (topic relevance, testable outcome focus on social anxiety symptoms, and some justification for VR and guidance). The main gap is the “line of reasoning culminating in the RQ, scientific relevance, and hypothesis”: the introduction provides information, but does not consistently synthesize it to a single, sharply formulated research question that is explicitly derived from theory and prior findings. Theoretical constructs (CBT vs exposure mechanisms vs VRET guidance mechanism) are mentioned, but not developed into a coherent argument predicting why therapist guidance should outperform self-guidance (and at which measurement points). For the rubric, criteria could be tightened by adding explicit anchors for what counts as “clear RQ” (e.g., comparison group(s) + key DV + timepoint) and “coherent reasoning” (e.g., require explicit synthesis sentences like “Taken together, X suggests…, therefore Y is tested”). Additionally, the rubric could benefit from clearer guidance distinguishing “somewhat coherent” vs “coherently argued” at introduction level, because current descriptors are somewhat overlapping and can be interpreted differently by graders.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section provides the core headings (Participants, Materials, Procedure) and includes several important elements such as recruitment source, diagnosis instrument (SCID-5), demographics, random assignment, exclusion criteria, VR hardware/software, and the primary outcome (LSAS-SR). However, the description is not fully coherent or complete for replication: the participant number is inconsistent with the sample sizes later implied, eligibility/diagnosis is described without the operational threshold for SAD, and some key implementation details (therapist guidance content, session structure, duration at-home setup, and exact exposure task progression) are missing or vague. The Materials section also mixes intervention characteristics and measurement details but does not clearly specify what differs between conditions beyond “guidance,” nor does it describe how the built-in therapist works compared to the real therapist. Overall, the design appears plausibly related to the stated comparison of guided vs self-guided VRET, but several methodological specifics are insufficient for a clear, correct, and complete methods account.
methods_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but contains several imprecise or incorrect formulations (e.g., “instructions... meant to mimic” without specifying content; several long sentences with multiple ideas). There are minor APA/style issues (e.g., inconsistent use of “Association” and inconsistent reference style; some spacing/formatting issues like “(n= 22)” and “and 36.7% male (n= 22)”). Paragraphing by subheading is clear, but there is redundancy and some missing precision that would improve clarity (especially in Procedure). APA citation usage is present but not consistently formatted, and some terms should be standardized (e.g., SCID-5 name, condition labels).
methods_rubric_feedback: Some rubric criteria would benefit from clearer anchors about what “complete and correct” means for Methods at this course level. For example, the band descriptors currently emphasize “nearly complete” vs “complete” but do not list which specific methodological elements must be present for full credit (e.g., allocation concealment, exact session scheduling, therapist involvement parameters, inclusion thresholds, operationalization of SAD severity). The transition between “coherent and somewhat related” and “coherent and clearly related” could also be more concrete by specifying evaluation points (e.g., whether the procedure matches the hypotheses and conditions). Finally, the rubric could better distinguish between (a) missing detail that limits replicability versus (b) conceptual/design errors; as written, both may compress into the same “somewhat comprehensibly” category, making grading somewhat subjective.
results_content_summary: The Results section reports a mixed-design ANOVA with main effects of time and condition and a time × condition interaction, followed by Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons. It also claims that assumptions (normality, homogeneity of variances, sphericity) were checked and that outliers were retained. However, it lacks the key quantitative reporting needed for replication and evaluation: there are no actual descriptive statistics by condition/time in the provided text (the referenced Table 1 is not sufficiently specified), and there are no reported group N by condition, F-test degrees of freedom consistency is questionable (F(2,116) with N=60 and yet F(1,58) is used), and the follow-up/outlier handling is described without linking it to the analyses reported. The conclusions about attrition, outliers, and score changes are therefore difficult to verify against the described methodology.
results_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but contains multiple precision issues (e.g., “results can be seen in the table below” without providing it; inconsistent wording such as “before vs after vs follow up” while later only mentions two time comparisons). There are grammar/formatting inconsistencies (e.g., “x and standard deviations,” inconsistent spacing around punctuation in p-values, and inconsistent capitalization of “Self-guided”/“Therapist-guided”). The section is not well-structured for scientific reporting because it mixes descriptive claims, assumption/outlier statements, and confirmatory analyses without clear separation or consistent reporting of what is actually in Table 1. APA compliance is incomplete: table reference/contents, effect size notation, and statistical reporting are not presented in a fully consistent APA-like format.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric could be tightened by explicitly requiring concrete anchors: e.g., stating that the section must include (a) descriptive statistics by condition/time, (b) the exact analysis model specification matching the design, and (c) a complete set of test statistics (F/df/p plus post-hoc comparisons) with consistency checks (df coherence). The band descriptors (“mostly correct, complete, coherent”) are somewhat subjective; adding examples of what “nearly complete” vs “complete” looks like (e.g., presence/absence of tables/figures, whether dfs are consistent) would reduce grader variance. “Demonstrating an in depth knowledge of statistical analyses” is not operationalized—adding specific subcriteria (effect sizes, assumption checks reported with relevant statistics, correction methods, and how outliers were treated analytically) would make the top band more measurable.
discussion_content_summary: The discussion addresses the study aim by summarizing that both therapist-guided and self-guided VRET reduce SAD symptoms, with therapist-guided showing larger short-term reductions and convergence at follow-up. It provides some interpretation grounded in prior work (e.g., human support, self-efficacy) and it offers a set of limitations and future directions. However, the reasoning is sometimes inconsistent with the paper’s own results framing (e.g., “in line with the hypothesis” despite claiming unexpected patterns), and several interpretations are not tightly linked to specific findings or mechanisms in a clearly structured line. Critical engagement with the most striking/odd pattern and its alternative explanations is present, but somewhat general and occasionally speculative.
discussion_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but includes multiple grammar issues and imprecise phrasing (e.g., missing/incorrect articles, “due the presence of,” “could potentially be explained due the absence,” “beyond post-treatment,” and occasional run-on sentences). APA compliance is weak in this section: references are not consistently formatted, and there are noticeable punctuation/character issues (e.g., “post‑treatment LSAS‑SR,” “e.g.,” inconsistent hyphenation). Paragraphing is mostly present but the argument is not always single-focused per paragraph, leading to redundancy and reduced clarity.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The rubric criteria are mostly clear, but some bands rely on qualitative judgments (“convincingly argued,” “relevant,” “somewhat coherent”) without concrete anchors such as minimum number/quality of theory-reasoning links or limitations/future research items. The Discussion criterion could be made more actionable by explicitly requiring: (a) correct and consistent restatement of the hypothesis vs. outcomes, (b) a clear comparison to at least the most central prior studies from the Introduction, and (c) at least two study-specific alternative explanations tied to the study design. Additionally, “critical reflection” could be anchored to observable indicators (e.g., specification of mechanism + why the study cannot test it + how that could bias the key comparison).
lang_style_rubric_feedback: To improve reliability, the rubric language & style criteria could use clearer anchors for what counts as “some” vs “numerous” APA/style errors, and how many errors typically map to each performance band. The descriptors mix several dimensions (grammar, redundancy, APA layout, vagueness) without specifying which should dominate the judgment when they conflict. Adding concrete examples (e.g., table/figure caption requirements, statistical formatting expectations, and citation placement rules) would make the bands more actionable and less subjective.
final_grade_justification: Although the discussion demonstrates a reasonable attempt to interpret guided vs self-guided effects, the paper’s scientific argumentation does not culminate in a sufficiently precise, theory-driven and testable research question. The Methods section is not replication-ready because key operational details (diagnostic thresholds, condition implementation specifics, session/exposure progression, and inconsistencies in sample sizing/eligibility) are missing or unclear. The Results section also lacks essential quantitative reporting and shows internal inconsistencies (e.g., degrees of freedom/sample size alignment), making the claims difficult to verify. Overall, the combination of under-specified methods and insufficiently supported results would likely prevent the student from achieving a passing standard for a future bachelor’s thesis.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides a broad overview of social anxiety disorder (SAD), its impact, and why accessible treatments matter. It then covers CBT and exposure therapy, and motivates VR exposure therapy as a potentially more feasible alternative to in vivo exposure. It also summarizes several relevant VRET studies, leading to the idea that guidance by a therapist might be important and that direct comparisons between therapist-guided and self-guided VRET are lacking. However, the scientific storyline is not fully coherent: key constructs/theory are sometimes loosely connected to the research question, and the research question/hypothesis are only clearly stated very late, with limited explicit derivation from the presented theoretical mechanisms.
intro_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but contains multiple grammar and spelling issues (e.g., inconsistent spacing, “Selfguided-VRET”, “oftentimes”, “RTC experimentin”, “Selfguided-VRET (self-guided…”, “but also requires…”). APA consistency is problematic: several references appear with inconsistent formatting and some citations are likely incomplete or not in correct APA style (e.g., “Kindred et al.. 2022”, “Pavlovian” framed via a questionable citation match, “Goetter et al., 2018” without context). Paragraph structure is mostly present, but topical sentences and transitions are sometimes weak, and there is redundancy in describing general effectiveness without adding new argumentative steps toward the specific RQ.
intro_rubric_feedback: Several rubric criteria are only partially met. The societal relevance is present early, but the line of reasoning culminating in a clear RQ/hypothesis is weak because the “why” (theoretical mechanism) and the “what” (exact RQ and testable predictions across time/conditions) are not tightly integrated until the end, and the hypothesis is stated in an underspecified way (only “post-treatment” despite mentioning pre/post/follow-up). The previous research section gives study summaries, but it does not consistently synthesize them as building blocks (e.g., what specifically is known about guidance mechanisms, adherence, expectancy violation/corrective feedback) and therefore the gap is argued more implicitly than convincingly. For the rubric to rate higher, the intro should explicitly: (1) state the research question clearly, (2) derive testable hypotheses directly from the theoretical accounts and the summarized evidence, and (3) clearly link design choices (including timing/measurement moments) to those hypotheses.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section includes the main headings (Participants, Materials, Procedure) and provides several key elements such as sample size, basic demographics, random assignment, exclusion criteria, VR hardware/software, and the LSAS-SR as an outcome measure. However, the study description is not sufficiently complete for replication and contains conceptual inconsistencies with the stated design in the broader paper context (e.g., it mentions taking the VR headset home in the self-guided condition, yet only 6 weekly sessions are described; it also does not clearly specify whether the “therapist” differs from the experimenter and how therapist guidance is standardized across participants). Additionally, important methodological details are missing or unclear: recruitment source and eligibility operationalization are vague, the SCID-5 timing/administration is not described, exclusion criteria thresholds are not given, and the specific VR exposure content/protocol (number of scenarios, duration, difficulty progression rules, adherence monitoring) is not described. The Procedure also mixes construct measurement administration with instruction delivery details in ways that reduce clarity.
methods_style_notes: Language is generally understandable, but several sentences are imprecise or overly informal (e.g., “takes home,” “female researcher,” “able to see what the participant was seeing”) and there are multiple grammar/wording issues (run-on sentences, missing commas, and inconsistent capitalization). APA formatting for this section is mostly acceptable structurally, but there are inconsistencies (e.g., “Association, 2022” vs. APA-style author formatting; long heading blocks; inconsistent use of hyphens and capitalization like “Self-Report Version (LSAS-SR)” vs later). Paragraphing is uneven, with many details packed into each numbered subsection, and there is some redundancy in describing instructions/sessions. Statistical/measurement reporting (scales, scoring) is described in good detail, but it is not consistently linked to the procedure timing and scoring rules with the same terminology throughout.
methods_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s Method criterion is broad (“participants, materials and procedures incomplete/incomprehensible and/or incorrect”), which makes it somewhat hard to calibrate and can lead to subjectivity when deciding what counts as “nearly complete” vs “complete.” Adding a checklist-style minimum set of replication-critical elements (e.g., inclusion/exclusion thresholds, exact randomization/allocation procedure, intervention protocol specifics, assessment time points, and adherence/implementation fidelity) would make scoring more concrete. The band descriptors could also be more anchorable by explicitly stating what “coherent and related to RQ” means in practice for common study designs (e.g., guided vs unguided VRET with waitlist/controls). Finally, the rubric would benefit from separating “clarity/replicability” from “accuracy of design logic,” since these often pull in different directions for student papers.
results_content_summary: The section reports that all participants (N=60) completed the study and that means/SDs were planned for baseline, post-treatment, and a 3-month follow-up. It describes a mixed-design ANOVA with time (3 levels) as within-subject and condition (2 levels) as between-subject, including assumption checks, effect sizes, and an interaction test. It then summarizes Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons for (a) pre vs post changes within each condition, (b) differential reductions across conditions, and (c) post vs follow-up change and final between-condition differences at follow-up. However, key result objects are missing or inconsistent with the described model (e.g., Table content is absent/unclear, degrees of freedom appear inconsistent with N and the model, and attrition/sample-size statements conflict with the earlier “all 60” while the text implies two conditions with outliers only in one condition/timepoint).
results_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but contains multiple precision and consistency problems (e.g., “x and standard deviations,” inconsistent use of timepoints in the model vs the table mention, and unclear attribution of what the table contains). Statistical reporting is written in prose, but the ANOVA degrees of freedom and the number of follow-up points are not clearly aligned with the stated sample size and condition structure. APA/formatting is incomplete for this excerpt: Table labeling is insufficient (no actual values shown), and there are minor punctuation/spacing issues (e.g., inconsistent spacing around “p =”). Paragraph structure is acceptable, though the section lacks clear subsections that cleanly separate descriptive results from inferential results.
results_rubric_feedback: The rubric for Results is directionally clear (correctness, completeness, coherence, relevance to stated design), but the “complete” threshold could be made more concrete. It would help to specify mandatory reporting anchors for this course (e.g., inclusion of at least one descriptive table with cell means/SDs, explicit test statistics with dfs that match the design, and a figure or clear statement of the interaction pattern). The rubric currently mixes “knowledge of statistical reasoning” with section-level criteria, which can make grading feel inconsistent unless it names specific statistical reasoning indicators (e.g., df sanity check, effect sizes, and clear post-hoc reporting). Finally, clarify how much “minor APA/stat formatting” can be tolerated before the band drops, since students may vary widely in template adherence even when the analysis is conceptually correct.
discussion_content_summary: The discussion summarizes that both therapist-guided and self-guided VRET reduce SAD symptoms, with a stronger short-term effect for therapist-guided and partial convergence at three months. It attempts to interpret the pattern with guidance-related mechanisms (support, demand characteristics) and a theoretical account for delayed self-guided improvement via self-efficacy. It compares the findings to prior VRET RCTs in general terms, and includes multiple limitations and future directions. However, several claims are not tightly grounded in the study’s (reported) statistical results, and the section introduces themes (e.g., “response bias at post-test” and self-efficacy) without clear linkage to the exact outcomes/timepoints and without engaging the research question in a structured, construct-level manner.
discussion_style_notes: Language is mostly understandable but contains frequent grammar/spelling and redundancy issues (e.g., “in this study,” “due the presence,” “follow up,” repeated phrasing, and several malformed sentences). APA/statistical and citation formatting is inconsistent, and there are missing/odd elements (e.g., “Table 1” style text appears at the end, and references/citations include some questionable ones for the stated claims). Paragraph structure is present but not always single-focus, and transitions are sometimes abrupt (e.g., shifting from results summary to mechanisms to limitations without clear signposting). Overall, the writing requires substantial editing for clarity, grammatical correctness, and APA consistency.
discussion_rubric_feedback: Your discussion makes a good start by stating the main takeaway and proposing plausible explanations, and it includes more than two study-specific limitations with concrete future research ideas. To move toward a higher band, the reasoning should be more tightly organized around each key result (short-term difference, within-condition change, follow-up convergence) and explicitly tied back to the specific hypotheses and theoretical mechanisms introduced in the introduction. Also, some interpretations need to be tempered or justified with clearer evidence from the results section (which comparisons actually reached significance at which timepoints). Finally, several discussion parts read as generic (“similar to established body of research”) rather than construct-level argumentation, and the APA/referencing consistency needs improvement to match the course expectations.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style criterion bundles several different concerns (scientific language, structure, APA mechanics, ambiguity/vagueness), which can make it hard to tell what specifically caused a transition between bands. Some descriptors (e.g., “numerous” vs “few” errors, or “vague or ambiguous statements in crucial parts”) would benefit from more concrete, countable anchors or examples. The bands for APA referencing/layout are close to each other, so defining what “hardly any” means in practice (e.g., permissible minor formatting deviations) would improve reliability. Finally, adding a clearer separation between language/grammar problems and APA/citation problems would make the grading more transparent and consistent.
final_grade_justification: Holistically, the paper falls below the passing threshold because the scientific storyline is not consistently linked to an explicit, well-derived research question/hypothesis until late, and the Methods section contains replication-breaking inconsistencies (e.g., headset-at-home vs described session structure) and missing operational details about screening, therapist standardization, and the VR exposure protocol. The Results section is also not reliably interpretable as written: key result objects are absent/unclear and reported degrees of freedom/sample-size details conflict with the described design assumptions. While the Discussion demonstrates conceptual engagement and includes limitations, several interpretive claims are not sufficiently grounded in clearly reported statistical outcomes. Given these issues, the paper would not likely enable a passing level of competence for a subsequent bachelor’s thesis the following year without substantial revision, so a fail is warranted.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides a broad overview of SAD prevalence, impairment, and the role of CBT/exposure, then motivates VR exposure therapy as a solution to barriers of in vivo exposure. It summarizes several experimental studies suggesting VRET’s effectiveness and introduces the gap regarding the need to compare therapist-guided versus self-guided VRET. However, the theoretical reasoning is not coherently developed into an explicit, testable line of argument for the specific research question, and key elements (precise RQ, clear hypothesis structure, and how the three measurement moments map onto the hypotheses) are presented only implicitly or inconsistently. Overall, the section’s storyline is present, but the “culminating” argument connecting theory → prior research → exact RQ/hypotheses is incomplete and somewhat confusing in wording and detail.
intro_style_notes: Language is generally readable but contains multiple grammar/wording issues (e.g., “most prominent,” “oftentimes,” “this led to increased research,” “selfguided-VRET” inconsistency), run-on sentences, and imprecise phrasing (“Pavlovian extinction model” used as if it directly specifies exposure mechanisms without clearly linking to constructs/hypothesis). APA/academic style compliance is uneven: citation formatting is inconsistent (spacing, occasional punctuation/citation placement), some sources appear with incorrect or inconsistent author/date formatting, and terminology is used with varying capitalization/hyphenation (VRET/TG-VRET/selfguided-VRET). Paragraph structure largely follows a common progression (background → theory → prior research → gap), but several paragraphs mix multiple ideas and lack clear topical sentences for the internal logic. Redundancy and clarity problems appear near the transition to the study aim (random assignment and measurements are described, but the RQ/hypotheses are not clearly aligned with those details).
intro_rubric_feedback: Several rubric criteria for Introduction are hard to score consistently because the bands rely on phrases like “somewhat convincingly argued for” and “very coherent,” which are subjective without concrete anchors (e.g., required minimum content such as explicit RQ sentence + explicit hypothesis derived from theory). The rubric could benefit from clearer sub-criteria separating (a) presence/clarity of RQ/hypotheses, (b) quality of literature synthesis vs mere summarization, and (c) whether theory is used again later to interpret/justify the hypothesis. Also, the distinction between “correct, somewhat coherent” and “correct, coherent” would be more reliable if described with observable markers (e.g., explicit construct definitions and a stated mechanism that makes different predictions for guided vs self-guided). Finally, the rubric currently does not penalize missing/unclear operational alignment (e.g., timepoints and which hypothesis is tested when) as explicitly as it could, even though that strongly affects whether students are able to write a scientific argument.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section contains most of the core subsections (participants, materials, procedure) and includes key descriptive details such as sample size, age, gender distribution, eligibility/exclusion criteria, and basic randomization. However, the study design is not clearly and consistently aligned with the described hypotheses/conditions: the number of conditions is ambiguous (two vs. “two conditions (30 each)”), yet the materials/procedure section describes therapist presence and home VR use in ways that are difficult to replicate precisely. Several important method details are missing or unclear (e.g., what “SAD medication” means operationally, whether VR exposure dosage/number of scenarios is identical across conditions, how the “built-in virtual therapist” differs from real therapist support, and how and when attrition is handled). Also, the LSAS-SR is described in general terms, but key administrative/scoring elements for this study (e.g., scoring procedure used, whether items are fear/avoidance summed exactly as described, and the intended timepoint naming) are not clearly specified.
methods_style_notes: Language is generally readable, but there are notable precision and consistency issues (e.g., “n=60” vs. “n=60) (n=60)”, inconsistent capitalization/formatting of subsections like 1.1/1.2/1.3, and some grammatical problems such as missing articles and long run-on sentences). APA compliance is incomplete: citations are inconsistently formatted (e.g., “Association, 2022” without an APA-style author string), and questionnaire instrument naming is not consistently handled (hyphenation/italics/standard naming). Paragraph structure mostly follows the rubric’s subsection logic, but redundancy appears (e.g., repeated explanation of therapist guidance/instructions) while critical procedural specifics are still omitted. Overall, the section would benefit from tighter, more technical phrasing and clearer separation between description of materials vs. procedural events.
methods_rubric_feedback: To improve alignment with the rubric bands, the Methods should provide a coherent, replicable operationalization of the two conditions: specify exactly what differs (guidance type, real-time vs. asynchronous feedback, therapist monitoring, exposure progression rules) and what is held constant (number/duration of exposures, scenario difficulty laddering, timing, environment, therapist contact hours). Add the missing procedural details needed to reproduce the study: exact randomization method and assignment concealment, whether intake sessions/home use include adherence monitoring, how the 3-month follow-up is scheduled and delivered, and what debrief/compensation procedures were (and whether they were identical). For materials, the VR content/protocol needs concrete description (scenario set, number of sessions’ exposure items, guidance script features, hardware model particulars) and for LSAS-SR you should specify the exact scoring implemented in this study rather than only general psychometric claims.
results_content_summary: The results section reports a mixed-design ANOVA framework (between-condition: self-guided vs therapist-guided; within-time: baseline, post-treatment, follow-up) and includes effect estimates (F, p-values, and partial eta-squared). It also describes assumption checks for normality, homogeneity of variances, and sphericity, and mentions outliers, with a decision to retain them. However, the quantitative reporting is incomplete and internally inconsistent with the described design and with the earlier mention of only 60 participants (yet ANOVA degrees of freedom suggest more data points). The section lacks the actual key descriptive table/values by time x condition and provides post-hoc comparisons without clearly specifying which contrasts map to the reported interaction and how follow-up comparisons were corrected/handled.
results_style_notes: Writing is generally understandable but contains several imprecise or incorrect phrases (e.g., “lower mean scores at post-treatment and follow-up” without providing numbers; “keep the outliers” without transparency about handling). APA/statistical formatting is inconsistent (spacing in p-values, use of symbols like η²p, and unclear table labeling). Paragraph structure is present (intro + analyses) but contains redundancy and unsupported statements (e.g., outliers described without quantification, table referenced but not provided).
results_rubric_feedback: The rubric for Results appropriately rewards correct, complete, coherent reporting linked to the stated design, but it could be more concrete about what minimum quantitative elements are expected (e.g., explicit descriptive means/SDs per condition × time, and how many follow-up comparisons including correction method). The bands (Developing/Adequate/Good) are still somewhat subjective because they depend on assessor interpretation of “mostly correct” without anchoring to a checklist. Consider adding explicit anchors for common pitfalls mentioned in course materials (e.g., degrees of freedom must match sample/structure; missing tables/figures count as incomplete reporting; correction method for post-hoc tests should be named). A further improvement would be to separate “statistical correctness” from “reporting completeness/coherence” so that partial credit is more transparent.
discussion_content_summary: The discussion clearly answers the core research aim in broad strokes: both guided and self-guided VRET reduced SAD symptoms, with therapist-guided showing stronger short-term effects and more similar outcomes at follow-up. It attempts to link findings to theory/mechanisms (e.g., demand characteristics/social desirability; self-efficacy) and includes multiple study-specific limitations and future directions. However, the reasoning sometimes conflicts with what the introduction/results appear to set up (e.g., the discussion claims “effects remaining quite stable at three months,” while also describing different trajectories), and several limitations are speculative or not tightly grounded in the paper’s actual design and measurement schedule. Overall, the section provides a reasonable structure but lacks consistently rigorous, construct-level integration with the theoretical framework and prior studies as required for a higher rubric band.
discussion_style_notes: Language is mostly understandable but contains frequent grammatical and precision issues (e.g., “VRET,” “vret,” “could potential,” “could be explained due the,” “because the presence of a therapist being available,” “We can not,” “Thirdly,”). Paragraphing is generally coherent, but there is redundancy and some unclear phrasing that blurs the main message. APA compliance is weak in this excerpt: it includes a “Reference List” block inside the discussion text, irregular citation formatting, and a lot of non-discussion material pasted at the end (tables/figures).
discussion_rubric_feedback: The rubric would benefit from more concrete anchors for “relevant and convincing” critical reflection—e.g., require at least two limitations that are clearly traceable to the study design/measurements and at least two future directions that directly follow from those limitations. Some wording is also ambiguous about what counts as “in depth knowledge of statistical analyses” in the Discussion; adding examples of acceptable vs unacceptable moves (e.g., interpreting effect direction/magnitude, engaging with unexpected patterns) would improve reliability across graders. Finally, several band descriptors are overlapping (e.g., “mostly coherent” vs “correct, nearly complete, mostly coherent”)—adding small bullets per level would make the scale easier to apply consistently.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric bands could be made more concrete by specifying which errors count as “numerous” vs “few,” and by separating grammar/spelling from APA/reference accuracy into clearer sub-bands. Several descriptors (e.g., “vague or ambiguous statements” and “redundancy”) are somewhat subjective; adding concrete examples or thresholds (like citation-format consistency or number of APA deviations per page) would improve reliability. Finally, the rubric could better distinguish between localized formatting issues (e.g., one broken heading/reference section) and systemic organization problems, since these have different impacts on reader comprehension.
final_grade_justification: Although the introduction and discussion show an overall plausible topic/story and the results section generally aims to match a mixed-design ANOVA, the core scientific reasoning is not coherently culminated into a clear, testable research question and hypothesis structure, and it remains difficult to map hypotheses to measurement timepoints. The Methods and Results contain substantial internal inconsistencies (e.g., ambiguous condition structure, insufficient operational detail, and quantitative reporting that appears inconsistent with the stated sample/design), which undermines the credibility of the statistical conclusions. The discussion provides a reasonable broad interpretation but relies on speculative or partially misaligned mechanisms and trajectories relative to what the study actually measured. Holistically, these issues are severe enough that the paper would likely not support a passing standard for a next-year bachelor’s thesis-level scientific writing task.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides a reasonable general overview of SAD, why it matters, and how CBT/exposure and then VRET could address practical barriers. However, the line of reasoning toward a specific, testable research question is incomplete: the core comparison (guided vs self-guided) is introduced late, and several key constructs and theoretical mechanisms are not clearly tied to the final hypothesis. The hypotheses are only partially stated (one post-treatment hypothesis is given, but not the full set of expectations implied by the described design, timing, and outcome measures). Overall, prior research is mostly summarized rather than synthesized into a coherent argument that culminates in a clearly justified RQ and a fully specified hypothesis set.
intro_style_notes: The section is generally readable, but there are frequent issues with academic precision (e.g., vague phrasing, occasional incorrect or unclear claims, and multiple missing or inconsistent transitions such as “This led to…”/“However…” without clear linkage). Grammar and punctuation errors appear often (spelling inconsistencies like “Selfguided/self-guided,” run-ons, and missing spaces), and citation formatting is inconsistent (e.g., “Kindred et al.. 2022” and non-standard spacing “Heinig et al.,2021”). Paragraph structure mostly follows a topical order, but there is some redundancy and drifting back to general background instead of maintaining a single storyline toward the research question. APA compliance is weakened by formatting inconsistencies and at least one problematic reference-year mismatch/unclear citation use.
intro_rubric_feedback: Several rubric criteria would benefit from clearer operationalization. For example, “line of reasoning culminating in the RQ” could be made more concrete by specifying what must be present (explicit RQ statement, explicit hypothesis set, and explicit gap resolution) rather than allowing subjective interpretation. The distinction between “somewhat coherent” and “mostly coherent” could be sharpened with examples (e.g., what counts as a logically derived hypothesis vs. a pasted-on hypothesis). Finally, “more than half of the references are irrelevant or outdated” could be given a clearer guideline on how to judge relevance (conceptual relevance to the RQ vs. general background relevance) to improve inter-rater reliability.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section is generally coherent and covers Participants, Materials, and Procedure, including diagnosis method (SCID-5), key demographics, random assignment, the main outcome measure (LSAS-SR), and the assessment timeline (pre, post, 3-month follow-up). However, important details needed for replicability are missing or unclear: the VRET dose/content (number and type of exposure scenarios), what exactly “WorldViz” and the VR therapist do operationally, and how the self-guided vs therapist-guided guidance differs in a standardized way. Several design elements also conflict or are incomplete (e.g., “two conditions (30 each)” despite later describing assignment between self-guided and therapist-guided, while no explicit mention of a waitlist/control in Methods). Exclusion criteria are described but medication/exposure-related criteria and the sampling procedure (screening for SAD severity thresholds, recruitment flow) are not sufficiently specified.
methods_style_notes: Language is mostly clear and readable, with a mostly consistent formal tone, but there are noticeable grammar issues (e.g., phrasing such as “asks how much fear or avoidance a person would feel if they did the activity stated” and inconsistent spacing around punctuation). APA-style structure is partially adapted (numbered subheadings are fine), but reference/APA formatting is not fully consistent (e.g., “Association, 2022” without proper author formatting/clarity, and incomplete variable naming consistency). Paragraphing is acceptable, yet some parts combine multiple methodological components in a way that reduces precision (e.g., Procedure mixes recruitment/instructions, assignment, and intervention delivery).
methods_rubric_feedback: Most criteria for a ‘coherent and somewhat related’ design are met (Participants, materials, procedure, and randomization are described), but the Methods are not yet complete and correct for this course level because key intervention and measurement-administration details are missing. To reach a higher band, you would need to explicitly report: (a) the full VRET protocol (session structure, number of exposures, progression rules, and therapist guidance content), (b) precise allocation/condition description consistent with the stated design (including any control/waitlist if applicable), and (c) more replicable participant-screening details (diagnostic thresholds, recruitment/screening workflow, medication status operationalization). At least one or two important details are currently unclear enough that another student likely could not fully reproduce the study as described.
results_content_summary: The section reports a mixed-design ANOVA framework and provides F-tests for the main effects and the interaction, along with Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons. However, the reporting is inconsistent with the described sample size and design: it states 60 participants total and 2 conditions, but the analysis uses degrees of freedom that do not clearly match those numbers (e.g., F(2,116) and F(1,58) with a two-condition setup). The description of outliers is vague (number of outliers is mentioned but no criteria, handling decisions, or whether they were retained/excluded in the reported analyses are specified), and the results lack the key descriptive statistics (means/SDs) referenced in Table 1. Overall, while the statistical logic is partially present, the results are not yet sufficiently complete and aligned with the stated methodology to be considered correct and replicable.
results_style_notes: The section has several clarity and precision issues (e.g., “Average scores on x”, repeated/unclear phrasing, and incomplete figure/table descriptions). Grammar and wording problems occur throughout (e.g., “the research has decided to keep the outliers in the study”, “the assumption of normality was met…” without indicating how it was tested), and there are missing line breaks/organization that make it harder to track the argument. APA/statistical formatting is partially correct for test reporting (F, p, η²p), but there are likely inconsistencies in spelling/terms and the section does not clearly present the required descriptive tables/values it refers to.
results_rubric_feedback: The rubric could be improved by making the alignment criterion between Methods and Results more explicit: for instance, specifying that degrees of freedom must match N/conditions/timepoints (or that inconsistency should automatically cap the score unless clearly explained). The Results criteria currently separate “correct/complete reporting” from “in depth knowledge,” but it is ambiguous how to grade when stats are presented yet key elements (descriptive tables, figures, or exact test specifications) are missing—adding concrete sub-bullets would reduce subjectivity. Also, the rubric does not explicitly address how to score poor or missing reporting of assumption checks and outlier handling (e.g., criteria, tests used, and whether they were included in the final analysis); adding a threshold would make grading more consistent across graders.
discussion_content_summary: The discussion is generally consistent with the reported pattern in the results: both groups improved, therapist-guided VRET showed larger immediate reductions, and effects converged by follow-up. The section provides an attempt at interpretation (therapist availability, demand/context effects, and self-efficacy) and compares the findings to prior VR-for-SAD research, culminating in a conclusion that matches the stated RQ. It also includes multiple, reasonably study-specific limitations and concrete future directions. However, it remains somewhat high-level in places (e.g., not always explicitly linking each claim back to specific hypotheses/findings), and several interpretations are speculative without clearly using the paper’s own statistical evidence (e.g., “benefits remained stable” / “convergence”).
discussion_style_notes: Language is mostly understandable and appropriately scientific, but there are frequent grammatical/spelling issues (e.g., 'could potentially be explained due the presence', 'to see whether there would be a difference', 'by directly comparing these two treatments, our research adds', 'we can not', 'effects remaining quite stable', missing spaces and inconsistent capitalization in the provided text). Paragraphing follows a recognizable structure (aims/findings → unexpected finding → comparison → limitations → future research → conclusion), with clear topical separation. APA compliance in this section is likely uneven: citations are present in-text, but the reference list excerpt suggests inconsistencies/formatting problems (e.g., questionable reference completeness/duplicates and at least one clearly problematic journal formatting artifact). Redundancy is moderate, and some sentences are imprecise (e.g., “results were in line with the hypothesis” without stating which hypothesis exactly).
discussion_rubric_feedback: Several rubric descriptors overlap and are hard to distinguish in practice. For example, the boundaries between “nearly complete and somewhat coherent” vs. “mostly coherent” vs. “complete and coherent” rely on subjective judgment without concrete sub-criteria (e.g., requirement to explicitly connect to each hypothesis/result). The “critical reflection” criterion is phrased fairly generally; it would help to specify what counts as “study-specific” vs. “generic limitations” and require at least two limitations that explicitly map to measurement/design weaknesses introduced earlier. Finally, the rubric mixes two goals in one band (“critical reflection” and “references used responsibly”)—separating these into distinct sub-criteria (argument quality vs. reference discipline) would make calibration easier.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style criteria use fairly clear bands, but the thresholds (e.g., “vague or ambiguous statements” count, “>10 APA errors”) are hard to apply consistently across graders because different graders may interpret what counts as an APA error or as “crucial parts.” The rubric could benefit from more concrete examples of what qualifies as an APA/layout error versus a minor formatting issue, and from specifying whether citation formatting problems and statistical formatting problems should be counted separately. It may also help to clarify how to weigh “frequent small grammatical issues” versus fewer but more disruptive language problems when placing a paper into bands.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides substantial background on SAD, exposure-based CBT, and why VRET might address barriers of in-vivo exposure, and it includes multiple relevant empirical papers about VRET. However, the paper’s core line of reasoning culminating in a clear, testable research question is not consistently built: the main rationale for the comparison (guided vs self-guided) is stated, but the research aim/RQ is only implicitly formulated and the operational design/hypothesis logic is somewhat abrupt. The theoretical explanations are present but remain somewhat loose (e.g., Pavlovian/extinction wording is not well connected to the guidance manipulation), and several causal transitions are phrased too strongly without fully substantiating the logic for why self-guided would be weaker or equal. The hypothesis is testable, but it is only one-sided and not fully aligned with the mentioned three measurement time points (pre, post, follow-up), leaving the reader unsure what exactly is expected at follow-up and how that follows from the theory/prior research.
intro_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but contains multiple spelling/grammar issues (e.g., 'Selfguided', 'Self-guided', 'o ftentimes', 'RTC', 'idiosyncratic fears' capitalization consistency) and some unclear or incomplete phrases (e.g., 'Koelen et al., 2022' introduced without clear integration). Paragraphing is mostly present, but several long paragraphs combine multiple argument steps, which weakens clarity of the argumentative storyline. APA usage is inconsistent (e.g., spacing before citations, double periods/typos like 'Levy et al., 2023 shows', and some questionable author/year formatting), and there are references to sources not clearly present in the provided required set for the course context. There is limited redundancy control: some treatment descriptions are repeated in near-similar wording (CBT/exposure) without adding new argument content.
intro_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s “line of reasoning culminating in the RQ/relevance/hypothesis” banding could be made more discriminative by separating (a) whether an RQ is explicitly stated from (b) whether it is clearly derived from evidence/theory. Similarly, the current descriptors mix “coherence” and “appropriateness” with “reference relevance,” which can be hard to judge consistently without explicit thresholds (e.g., what counts as ‘somewhat coherent’ vs ‘mostly coherent’). Adding a short checklist of minimum introduction requirements per band (e.g., explicit RQ, explicit hypothesis, alignment with design/time points) would reduce ambiguity. Finally, the criterion mentions outdated/irrelevant references but doesn’t define what proportion qualifies as ‘more than half’ vs ‘up to date’ in a consistent way; concrete examples or percent cutoffs would improve reliability across graders.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section contains several key elements (participants with eligibility/exclusion, materials/instruments, randomization, and a clear pre/post + 3-month follow-up assessment schedule) that make the study broadly replicable. However, important details are missing or inconsistent: allocation is described as “two conditions” (self vs therapist-guided) despite the earlier mention of n=60 split into two groups (no waitlist/third arm), and recruitment/diagnostic/medication criteria are not fully specified (e.g., “medication to treat SAD” lacks operational rules). The procedure lacks the concrete intervention protocol details needed to judge comparability across conditions (exact number/length/content of exposure exercises, progression criteria, therapist role/amount of guidance, adherence, and whether any safety behaviors were allowed/forbidden). Overall, it is mostly coherent and partly complete, but not “complete and correct” for a course expecting a near-replicable psychological RCT method.
methods_style_notes: Language is generally clear but sometimes imprecise (e.g., “two differences being…” while several elements vary; “WorldViz” and “Oculus Rift” described but implementation details are thin). There are some grammar/spelling issues and minor awkward phrasing (e.g., “with each session progressively becoming more challenging,” “in their VR headset,” “full knowledge about the research”). APA-wise, subsections are consistent, but citations/formatting are inconsistent (e.g., “Association, 2022” vs full APA style not fully applied; “Heimberg et al., 1999” vs earlier DSM reference). Paragraphing is mostly structured, but Procedure mixes procedural and intervention-description content.
methods_rubric_feedback: To improve, the rubric would benefit from clearer expectations on what counts as “complete” in Methods for this course (e.g., minimum intervention protocol specifics: number of exposure scenarios, progression rule, therapist guidance components, and adherence handling). The bands distinguish between “somewhat related” vs “related” but don’t explicitly mention checking design/hypothesis alignment (e.g., ensuring the stated number of conditions/arms matches the RQ). Adding 1–2 concrete examples of what would move a paper from “nearly complete” to “complete and correct” would make the scale easier to apply consistently. Finally, a clarification whether reviewers should penalize conceptual inconsistencies (e.g., “two conditions” vs an RCT template that often includes a waitlist arm) as “incorrect/incoherent” would sharpen the lower bands.
results_content_summary: The section reports that there was no attrition and that all participants’ data were analyzed, then describes planned descriptive statistics and a mixed-design ANOVA. It includes key inferential outputs (main effects of time and condition, and the time × condition interaction) with effect sizes and p-values, followed by Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons aligned to the interaction. However, the results section is incomplete and internally inconsistent with respect to the described sample size/conditions and the planned factors: the ANOVA is reported with degrees of freedom and two-condition labels, but the narrative still uses a follow-up/three-timepoint structure without providing the required condition × time means/SDs in a usable table. Finally, the section discusses outliers but does not specify whether outlier handling affected the ANOVA, nor does it clearly report the actual descriptive results that would support the claims about baseline comparability and change patterns.
results_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but contains several imprecisions and grammar issues (e.g., “no attrition or invalid data,” “follow up 3 months later,” “Between pre- and post-treatment,” and “The research has decided…”). The section has clear headings, but the table is not actually provided (only a title and partial table reference), which reduces clarity/precision in presenting the results. APA/statistics formatting is uneven: degrees of freedom and F-statistics are inconsistently written (and the df appear incompatible with the earlier “60 participants” / “self-guided vs therapist-guided” description), and some terminology is redundant or vague (“appropriate manner,” “research has decided”).
results_rubric_feedback: The rubric would benefit from clearer separation between “reporting required results elements” and “having correct statistical reporting,” because some parts here are present (ANOVA outputs and post-hocs) while the section is missing/unclear on core descriptive tables and consistency with the stated design. The criteria for Results mention in-depth statistical knowledge, but the rubric doesn’t specify how to grade problems like mismatched degrees of freedom, inconsistent sample sizes, or unreported means/SDs—these can be treated very differently depending on severity. Adding concrete examples (e.g., what counts as a “complete” results report for a mixed ANOVA: at minimum descriptives by condition × time, F(df) for each tested effect, and post-hoc details with correction and direction) would make the band distinctions sharper. Finally, the rubric could clarify whether “outliers discussion” belongs in Results or Discussion and how much detail is expected in Results when outliers are handled (kept vs removed).
discussion_content_summary: The discussion restates the aim and summarizes the main outcome that therapist-guided VRET reduced social anxiety more than self-guided VRET post-treatment, while effects converge at follow-up. It attempts to explain these patterns using plausible mechanisms (e.g., therapist support, self-efficacy) and links some claims to prior literature. However, several parts are inconsistent with the study/results you provided earlier (especially: stating three-month follow-up effects and “long term” comparisons despite the provided results section not clearly supporting those patterns), and the discussion does not clearly address theoretical constructs from the Introduction in a structured way. The limitations and future directions are more concrete than the interpretation, but some are phrased in a way that sounds speculative without fully tying back to the study design and key unexpected findings.
discussion_style_notes: Language is generally understandable but contains noticeable grammar and phrasing issues (e.g., missing/incorrect articles and word forms like “could potentially be explained due the presence of a therapist” and “considering that previous research has shown…”). Paragraphing is mostly logical, but there is some redundancy (e.g., re-stating similar conclusions multiple times) and some unclear transitions (e.g., from “long term” framing to specific post vs follow-up claims). APA compliance issues appear in citation formatting and reference list structure (e.g., some entries look incomplete/incorrect, and in-text citations are used inconsistently). Overall, the section reads less like an argument that carefully builds on the Results and more like a generic discussion scaffold.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The discussion banding is somewhat hard to apply because it relies on “correctness” of the main conclusion and the quality of critical reflection, but the rubric doesn’t specify how to judge inconsistency between stated design elements (e.g., follow-up) and reported analyses when grading Discussion alone. The criteria for “at least 75% of references used responsibly” are also ambiguous: does this mean relevance, correct factual statements, or proper integration with claims? Finally, the rubric would benefit from clearer separation between (a) engaging with unexpected findings, (b) linking back to theory from the Introduction, and (c) depth of limitations/future directions, since currently a single overall label covers multiple distinct skills.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric uses thresholds (e.g., “>10 different APA errors” or “<5 vague statements”) that are hard to apply consistently because “different errors” and “crucial parts” are not operationalized. It would help to separate (a) frequency vs (b) severity of APA/grammar issues, since a few severe citation/layout mistakes can impair understanding more than many minor typos. Consider adding clearer examples for what counts as a “vague or ambiguous statement” and what qualifies as an “APA referencing or layout” error to improve inter-rater reliability.

intro_content_summary: The introduction provides broad societal/clinical relevance for social anxiety disorder and motivates using exposure-based interventions and then VRET. It includes a theoretical discussion (CBT and exposure mechanisms) and summarizes several RCTs to argue that VRET is promising and therapist guidance may matter. However, the line of reasoning becomes partially incoherent: the research gap and exact research question are not clearly articulated, and the paper’s hypotheses are not fully and precisely derived (e.g., timing/interaction with the waitlist is unclear). Overall, the section is on the borderline between “developing” and “adequate”: relevant content is present, but the theoretical-to-hypothesis chain and the RQ/hypothesis testability/precision are insufficiently structured.
intro_style_notes: The writing is understandable and mostly grammatically sound, but there are frequent punctuation/spacing issues (e.g., double spaces, missing spaces in “Selfguided-VRET”), capitalization inconsistencies, and a few vague or incorrect formulations (“Pavlovian extinction model” as stated, “Levy et al. shows…” without clear role in the argument). Several sentences are long and sometimes rely on informal phrasing (“This is a shame”, “increasing research shows”), and there is some redundancy (e.g., multiple mentions of effectiveness without adding new argumentative steps). Citations are generally present, but reference formatting/consistency is inconsistent (e.g., “Kindred et al.. 2022”, “Koelen et al., 2022” with unclear relevance). Paragraph structure mostly follows a logical progression, but transitions are weak around the gap/hypothesis and the final study description.
intro_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s “line of reasoning culminating in the RQ, scientific relevance and/or hypothesis” could be made more concrete by specifying whether the RQ must be explicitly stated as a specific question and whether hypotheses must be stated in testable form (e.g., direction, timepoint, and comparisons). The band descriptions distinguish “somewhat coherent” vs “coherent” vs “very coherent” largely qualitatively; adding an observable checklist (e.g., RQ present in 1–2 sentences; gap stated before RQ; hypotheses derived from theory and aligned with design) would reduce ambiguity. The criterion about “references are relevant and up to date” would benefit from clearer operational thresholds (e.g., how many citations qualify as “relevant” in a typical intro length, and whether missing core articles automatically caps the score). Finally, consider splitting “scientific relevance” into (a) problem importance and (b) gap novelty, so graders can score these separately rather than blending them.
methods_content_summary: The Methods section is largely coherent and appropriately connected to a two-condition (self-guided vs therapist-guided) VRET design with SAD diagnosis using SCID-5 and outcomes measured with LSAS-SR at pre-, post-, and 3-month follow-up. It includes several key elements (sample size, basic inclusion/exclusion, random assignment, instrument description, session timing/duration, and compensation). However, it omits or blurs several crucial replicability details: the design also needs a clear waitlist/control (not present here), allocation/stratification details are only partially specified, and the procedure lacks operational detail on the exposure exercises (number/content per session, therapist guidance specifics, adherence monitoring, and standardization across conditions). There are also inconsistencies between the introduction’s stated two-to-three-arm logic and these methods, and some materials details are too vague (e.g., WorldViz “special software” and how the virtual therapist operates beyond generalities).
methods_style_notes: Writing is generally understandable and uses mostly scientific language, but there are grammar/wording issues (e.g., awkward phrases like “The self-rated test contains 24 items that asks…”, and occasional inconsistent spacing around symbols like “n= 22”). APA compliance is incomplete: the citations are irregular (e.g., “Association, 2022)” without clear author formatting), and there are no consistent in-text reference patterns for key claims (e.g., reliability/validity cited via Heimberg et al., 1999 but the edition/match is unclear). Paragraph structure is mostly aligned with subsections (Participants/Materials/Procedure), but within-sections several sentences mix description of materials vs procedural steps, and some redundancy/ambiguity reduces precision (e.g., “guidance… only two differences being…” while other differences also exist).
methods_rubric_feedback: The rubric’s Method criterion is mostly appropriate, but it bundles several distinct skills (design coherence, completeness of participant allocation/inclusion/exclusion, and replicability of materials/procedure) into one band description, making it hard to distinguish between “complete but imperfect” vs “partially incomplete but coherent.” Consider adding explicit sub-criteria or checkboxes for (a) control/comparison conditions clarity, (b) instrument administration schedule (where/when), and (c) intervention protocol fidelity (dose, session components, therapist behaviors/standardization). Also, the “unnecessary details” clause could be clarified with examples (e.g., which kinds of detail are typically unnecessary for this course vs which kinds are essential for replication). Finally, the bands describing “two or one important details” could benefit from concrete examples of what counts as an “important” missing detail at this course level (e.g., number of exposure tasks per session, therapist guidance protocol, adherence handling).
results_content_summary: The section reports a mixed-design ANOVA with condition (between-subject) and time (within-subject), and provides the key omnibus F-tests with effect sizes for main effects and the interaction.
